**Prometheus**. Release me, Jupiter, for I have suffered heavy pain. **Jupiter**. You say I should release you? When you should rightfully wear heavy fetters and have the entire Caucasus <note>The Caucasus Mountains, where Prometheus was famously chained by Zeus as punishment.</note> lying upon your head; furthermore, not only should sixteen vultures gnaw at your entrails, but you should also be deprived of your eyes—those very eyes with which you previously made men out of this clay, stole fire, and forged women <note>A reference to the creation of Pandora, the first woman in Greek mythology, often depicted as a punishment for mankind.</note>. Through which you also deceived me in the dividing of the meat, when you covered bones with the fatty skin and set them before me, but kept the best for yourself <note>Prometheus tricked Zeus into choosing the less desirable parts of an animal sacrifice, ensuring that humans could keep the good meat for themselves.</note>. What indeed should one do with you? **Prometheus**. Why have I not sufficiently atoned? Since I have been fastened to the Caucasus for so long, and have had that wicked bird, the harmful eagle, consuming my liver. **Jupiter**. In this, it is still the least of the things you must suffer. **Prometheus**: Yet, Jupiter, you shall not release me without reward; rather, I will inform you of a dangerous thing. **Jupiter**: With...

# Introduction to Alchemy
## that is, Guidance to Alchemy drawn together from various Alchemical writers.

->Preface of the little book.<-

<term>Alchemy</term> is the most magnificent and excellent among all other arts, and the very core and marrow of all natural <term>philosophy</term>. It was pursued by the ancients with the highest diligence; for even the <term>Egyptians</term>, as <term>Suidas</term> <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist whose work includes early historical references to alchemical practices in Egypt.</note> testifies, practiced this and derived no small benefit from it. For this reason, some attribute its beginning to <term>Hermes</term>; for under his name the <term>Emerald Tablets</term> <note>original: "Tabulae Smaragdinae"; a legendary cryptic text that was believed to contain the secret of the "prima materia" and its transmutations.</note> are shown—certainly a small but correctly conceived booklet regarding the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapide philosophorum"</note>—in which the highest means and end goal of the dwelling of the philosophical stone are indicated. Yet after him, <term>Aristotle</term> and <term>Theophrastus</term>, as the most excellent <term>philosophers</term>, illuminated this art with honorable writings. The <term>Arabs</term>, however, as in other matters of the noble arts, have also used great understanding and diligence in this, writing books about it and thus improving and expanding the art for posterity. Among these, <term>Geber</term> and <term>Avicenna</term> are primarily counted, though Geber rightly maintains the advantage here, for he diligently described the entire alchemical art in five books, and alongside them also the <term>instruments</term> <note>original: "Instrumenta"</note>, wherein he...

<summary>This page provides a formal definition of alchemy as the purification of "lower" metals into "superior" ones and begins a historical preface tracing the art's origins from Egypt and Hermes Trismegistus to Arabic scholars like Geber.</summary>

## Of the Definition and Name of Alchemy

**Alchemy** is called by its right name among the Greeks **Chumia** or **Chimia**, <note>original: "Xumia Chimia"</note> that is **fusoria** <note>original: "fusoria"; the art of melting or casting.</note> or the art of smelting. This is because it deals with metals and their relatives, namely salts and alums, which flow in the fire. The Greeks, however, borrowed this name from the **Egyptians** and, according to their custom, added the article <note>Referring to the Arabic prefix "Al-" added to the Greek "Khemia."</note> and called it **Alchemy**. One person has defined this noble art one way, and another person another way. To put it another way, **Alchemy** is an art which teaches how to transform all kinds of metal, one into the an-

<column-break/>

-der, and to give it a nature equal to it; in Medicine. Another says: **Alchemy** is an art which teaches how one should make and prepare an **Elixir** <term>Elixir</term> <note>From the Arabic *al-iksir*, a potent substance used to catalyze the transformation of metals or heal the body.</note>. This **Elixir**, when it is cast upon metals or "imperfect bodies," <note>In alchemical theory, "imperfect bodies" refers to base metals like lead, tin, or copper, which are "sick" and need to be "cured" into gold.</note> makes them perfect. It is easy to see how excellent this art is, because in a short time it may bring forth that which Nature cannot accomplish in many years.

## Concerning the Principles of the Mastery <note>original: "Magisterij"; referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy</note>, which one should use in the work of Alchemy.

### The First Chapter.

After one has attained a knowledge of natural things from the principles of philosophy, one must not remain with this alone, so that our study does not lose its hoped-for benefit; we must proceed further toward the completion of the Work. For just as Theory <note>original: "Theorica"</note> without Practice <note>original: "Practica"</note> is completely and utterly useless, so too is Practice without Theory blind. Therefore, in order to have something perfect, one must have both together. For only thus may one finally reach the desired goal; otherwise, where one is lacking, the Work remains imperfect and unaccomplished. Now, the labor of this Art consists of

<column-break/>

these principles with which the artist works in this Mastery, namely: **Sublimation**, **Descension** <note>a form of distillation where vapors are forced downward</note>, **Distillation**, **Solution** <note>dissolving</note>, **Coagulation**, **Fixation** <note>making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, and **Ceration** <note>softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>.

## Concerning Sublimation.

To sublimate <note>original: "Sublimirn"</note> is to drive a dry thing upward through the power of fire, so that it clings to the top of its vessel. Sublimation is useful for purifying the "waters" <note>here referring to chemical liquids or spirits</note>, for the fine and clear parts are separated from the coarser parts, and thus the spirits are cleansed of their heaviness. There is yet another reason for this: namely, so that the "combustibility" <note>the quality of being easily burnt away or ruined</note> might be taken from it, as may be known regarding **Arsenic** <note>original: "Arsenico"</note>. For before sublimation, it burns easily, but after sublimation, it does not allow itself to be ignited. The same distinction can be seen with **Sulfur**. However, Sublimation is of many kinds, just as there are many kinds of spirits. For one happens through strong glowing heat, another with moderate heat, and yet another with gentle fire. One sublimates Arsenic and Sulfur with a gentle fire because their most subtle parts are united with the coarse; otherwise, their entire substance would rise up together without any purification—indeed, it would become black and burnt. Therefore, one must moderate the heat in the right proportion and the fire <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "die feue," likely intending "die feuer" (the fire).</note>

## Concerning Descension

Descension <note>A method of distillation where vapors or molten liquids are forced downward through a filter or perforated vessel.</note> is the driving downward of a solid thing through fire and melting, which one might call liquefaction <note>original: "Liquifacion"</note>. Descension was invented for this reason: that one might secure a matter in that same vessel which is called the *Chemical Descensory* <note>original: "Descensorium Chemicæ"</note>, and it then flows descending downward through the holes, just as one must and can see is required. The second reason is that the melting bodies <note>original: "Corpora"</note> are thereby protected from burning, after they have been reduced to their *calx* <note>original: "Calce"; the powdery oxide or residue left after heating a metal</note>, and all dross must be removed as soon as it is reduced. This is accomplished conveniently through the *descensory*. The third reason is that one cleanses the *bodies* <note>original: "Corpora"</note> from all foreign impurities, for the crushed body sinks purely downward and leaves everything that is not of its essence lying in the upper part of the vessel <note>original: "Poliren"</note>. Thus, one should "descend" a body that we wish to purify, such as when one granulates it or files it small / and adds *calx* to it / which 

<meta>catchword: one does not</meta>

---

<page-num>15</page-num>

one does not intend to combine, and it then flows in such a way. We find that through this the *bodies*—if the work is frequently repeated—are cleaned, yet not perfectly, though it is still useful.

## Concerning Distillation

Distilling is the driving of watery vapors upward. *Distillation* <note>original: "destillatión"</note> occurs in two ways: the first carries the vapors upward through the *alembic* <note>original: "alembick"; a traditional alchemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>; the other drives them downward *by descension* <note>original: "per descensúm"</note>, through which the *oil* <note>original: "Oleúm"</note> and the *vegetable essence* <note>original: "Vegetabilitas"; the volatile life-force of plant matter</note> are drawn. One distills so that volatile things may be separated from heaviness and turbidity and everything may be protected from putrefaction. In distillation through the *alembic*, the pure water is separated from the dregs. In [descending] distillation, however, one extracts the pure oil as it is in its nature.

## Concerning Calcination

*Calcination* <note>original: "Calcinatión"</note> is the burning of a thing by fire, such that one removes the moisture that holds the parts together. *Calcination* was invented so that the combustible, destructive, and burning parts and *spirits* <note>original: "spiritús"</note> are taken away by the fire. There are many kinds of *calcination*, according to the various ways they are required. Those which...

But because there are three kinds of imperfect bodies: the first includes Copper <note>original symbol: ♀</note> and Iron <note>original symbol: ♂</note>; the other includes Tin <note>original symbol: ♃</note> and Lead <note>original symbol: ♄</note> (all of which allow themselves to be calcined), their state and the transformation of their *spirit* is taken away through a calcining fire. Without these means, however, they do not stand at all. When one pursues the preparation of the "quiet histories" <note>likely referring to the stable, finished products of the chemical process</note> through them, the bodies are always made pure through often repeated *calcinations* <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove impurities or change its physical state</note>. A single calcination of them is done so that one may harden them and make them endure the glowing heat more easily.

## Concerning Dissolution

Dissolution <note>original: "Solution"</note> is to transform a dry thing into water. And this happens through subtle means and the intake of subtle waters that are without any dross, such as distilled vinegar, wine, grapes, and those four <note>likely referring to the four grades of strength or the four elements in liquid form</note>. But Dissolution was invented so that one might make the things that still have a "way in" <note>an entrance for chemical change</note> even more subtle <margin>more deeply</margin>. However, a thing which is dissolved and has the nature and quality of a hide or a claw or the like, its property is that it provides a fluidity before the *vitrification* <note>the process of turning into glass</note> or becoming glass.

<meta>catchword: Concerning Coagulation</meta>

## Concerning Coagulation

Coagulation is the reduction of a liquid thing into a dry substance through the removal of moisture <gloss>drying out</gloss>. There are two kinds of this invention: one is the *induration* or hardening of Quicksilver <note>Latin: "Argentum Vivum"</note>; the other is the discharge of the dissolved Mercury or the watery parts mixed therein. Quicksilver is coagulated in two ways: one is when one takes away from it all its innate moisture; the other is when one *inspissates* <note>thickens by evaporation</note> its moisture until it hardens. But its *congelation* <note>freezing or solidifying</note> is strange and extensive, of which more is spoken in other places.

## Concerning Fixation

Fixation <note>original: "Fixion"</note> is to make a thing that flees the fire <gloss>stay with it</gloss>—that is, making what is volatile become something that <gloss>remains</gloss> in the same fire. But Fixation was invented so that one might make the *tincture* <note>the transformative alchemical substance</note> and the *alteration* permanent within the transmuted or altered body, so that the same does not fade away. However, these are of many kinds, according to the various properties of the things one intends to fix: such as Lead, Tin, Iron, and Copper <note>original symbols: ♄ ♃ ♂ ♀</note> and their like *spirits*, which are then Sulfur and Arsenic in the first degree, Mercury in the second, and in the third Pearl <note>Latin: "Margareta"</note>, Magnesia, and Tutty <note>original: "Tutia"; a zinc oxide residue from smelting</note> and the like. One fixes the imperfect bodies through...

<summary>This page defines four major alchemical operations: Calcination (purification by fire), Dissolution (turning solids to subtle liquids), Coagulation (solidifying mercury), and Fixation (making volatile substances heat-resistant).</summary>

## Concerning Ceration

Ceration <term>Ceratio; the process of softening a hard substance to a wax-like consistency</term> is the softening and reviving of a hard, inflexible thing. Sometimes, however, it is found that one must prepare <note>original: "praepariren"</note> a thing for "entry" into the "body" <note>the metal or base material being worked upon</note>. This always proceeds by placing the material on the fire, which must be ground <term>leviren; to grind into a fine powder</term> and then sublimated <term>sublimiren; to heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</term> as often as necessary until it remains stable <note>original: "Fix"</note> and refined within the vessel. However, this [stability] should not be granted unless it is perfectly purified of everything that might cause the destruction of the ores. But it is believed that nothing is better than to fix the furnace with Oil of Tartar <term>Oleo Tartari; a solution of potassium carbonate used as a chemical reagent</term>, and that the proper and necessary ceration be performed with it at all times.

# Concerning the three Orders or grades of Medicines, besides the Elixir

## The first Chapter

A "Medicine" <note>In alchemy, a 'Medicine' refers to a substance—often the Philosopher's Stone or a derivative—capable of 'healing' or perfecting base metals into gold or silver</note> is so named because it effects a change, whether great or small, in the body upon which it is used. It is distinguished or divided into three grades or orders.
The first includes all preparations of minerals which, when applied to imperfect bodies, causes them to take on another nature, yet does not yield anything permanent, because the "elixirated" <term>Elexirierte; transformed by an elixir</term> or transmuted work tends to fade and perish. Always, the [impression] of the medicine...
<meta>catchword: impression</meta>

---

...impression disappears from it completely and utterly. Such are all the "whitening" <note>original: "dealbirende"</note> or <unclear>non-universal</unclear> sublimations <term>Sublimationes; the process of purifying a substance by vaporizing it</term> of Copper <term>Veneris</term> and Iron <term>Martis</term> which are not "fixed" <note>meaning they remain volatile and the change is not permanent</note>. Similarly, this includes every "Increase of Gold" <term>Augmentum Solis</term> or Silver <term>Lunae</term> or Copper <note>original symbol: ♀</note>; if they are mixed together, the sum may well produce a surface tint <term>anstrich; a superficial coating or color</term>, but it is unstable, and is more like dross through its...
<margin>Opinion</margin>
...touching <term>anrührung; the act of applying the alchemical agent to the metal</term>. In the second order of Medicine, we name every preparation which, when applied to the imperfect bodies, changes them well; however, because that other perfection is still lacking, and some [imperfections] remain within in terms of the strength of their properties. Such is the Calcination of Bodies <term>Calcinatio Corporum</term>, because it is taken from among all volatile things; such is the form of the Medicine which permanently colors Silver <note>original symbol: ☾</note> yellow, or makes Copper <note>original symbol: ♀</note> permanently white—yet everything in them still contains something destructible.
The third order of Medicine I call every preparation <term>Praeparation</term> which, when cast upon the bodies, removes all destructibility <term>zerstörligkeit</term> and makes them entirely perfect without any defect. This, however, is the only one [of its kind], and through it, one is freed from the effort of seeking the ten medicines of the second order <term>secundi ordinis</term>. There, one also calls the work of the first grade "the lesser."

### Robertus: A way or means by which one can <term>rubify</term> <note>original: "rubificiren"; the alchemical process of turning a substance red, often associated with the final stages of the Great Work</note> every prepared <term>body</term> <note>original: "corpus"; the solid, physical matter or base metal being worked upon</note> and every prepared <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritum"; the volatile essence or gaseous form of a substance</note>.

Take a body and the spirit belonging to it, which you desire to rubify or make red, and <term>imbibe</term> <note>to soak or saturate a solid with a liquid</note> the same body or spirit with patience to turn it red, using a clear water; through this, your desired substance will then harden or <term>coagulate</term> in the glow of the fire. Repeat this as many times as necessary until you see that the work has become as red as a <term>hyacinth</term> <note>a reddish-orange gemstone, likely zircon, used here to describe a specific deep red color</note> and the grains glow in the fire.

### Robertus: How one can make a red water which remains <term>fixed</term> <note>stable and non-volatile; able to withstand the heat of the fire without evaporating</note> and permanent.

Take 1 <term>ounce</term> <note>symbol: ℥</note> of <term>Salmiak</term> <note>Sal ammoniac; ammonium chloride, used to clean metals and promote chemical reactions</note> and grind it or make it into a meal with 4 ounces of fine <term>Atrament</term> <note>a black, metallic sulfate, often iron vitriol or "ink-stone," used for making dyes and acids</note>. Pour a moderate amount of vinegar over it, roughly 4 ounces. Distill it ten times, taking fresh Atrament each time; thus you will obtain a very beautiful water, as red as the purest <term>gold-blood</term>. With this water, you can <term>tinge</term> <note>to color or fundamentally change the appearance of a metal</note> all bodies that you hang or cast into it. This tincture will never be lost, but will remain forever constant and red.

### Robertus on the same matter.

Take a pound <note>symbol: ℔ p.</note> of <term>calcined</term> <note>burned to a powder or oxide through high heat</note> Atrament and grind it with as much strong vinegar as there is Atrament, so that you obtain the very best ripening <term>Vitriol</term> <note>sulfate of a metal, such as iron or copper, often appearing as green or blue crystals</note>. Then distill it through an <term>alembic</term> <note>a classic two-part distillation apparatus</note>. You must do this ten times, always renewing the Atrament. When you have renewed it for the tenth time, the Atrament will become brittle and <unclear>as</unclear> dry. If, by the tenth time, it has not yet succeeded or worked well, then do it more often and for as long as it takes to reach that state. For it colors or tinges all bodies when allowed to precipitate, so that it remains permanent and red forever.

### Robert’s Water of Atrament

Take 2 ounces of <term>Weinstein</term> <note>Cream of Tartar; potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking used as a flux</note> and grind it with fresh or strong vinegar. Place it in a steady blast of fire until it is completely glowing, and let it lie for <unclear>five</unclear> hours until it becomes thoroughly red. Then cast it again into distilled fennel or vinegar. Then <term>sublime</term> <note>the process of heating a substance into a vapor and collecting the solid deposit it forms</note> the water twelve times, and you will obtain the Water of Atrament, which will be an exceedingly beautiful red.

## Another [Method]

He took pigeon dung and <term>Litharge</term> <note>original: "Litargirium"; lead oxide</note> along with the silver-glaze, and let them burn to powder in a new box with a wick that had not been used. But he had previously consumed the lead entirely; he took as much **Lead** <note>♄</note> as he wished, made it warm, and threw it into <term>Yellow Water</term> <note>original: "Aquam lüteam"</note> or sulfur water, and did this many times. Afterwards, he melted or cast it with <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>original: "Sal Armoniac"; ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note> and salt; he reported that he found the <term>Lead</term> <note>Saturnum</note> to be beautiful and white like silver.

## How one can make a feather-gold "sweet."
<note>"Feather-gold" (Feders Goldt) refers to gold in thin, light flakes. "Sweetening" in alchemy usually means removing corrosive acids or refining the metal to make it more malleable and pure.</note>

Take 1 <term>Lot</term> <note>a weight unit, about 14-15 grams</note> of sublimated <term>Mercury</term> <note>symbol: ☿</note> and ½ pound of salt that has been evaporated, finely calcined, and then <unclear>purified</unclear>. ## To make a descensum.
<note>A "descensum" (distillation by descent) is a process where a substance is heated in an upper vessel so that the refined liquid flows downward through a hole into a lower container.</note>

Take a small vessel or <term>Crucible</term>, and make a tiny little hole in the bottom. Set it with the bottom upon another crucible. Seal or wall it up tightly everywhere—both the joint and the path—with <term>Potter's Clay</term> or loam. First, give it a gentle fire. Afterward, increase the fire until everything that is in the uppermost vessel has passed entirely down into the lower box-crucible, while the glowing coals lie all around the upper vessel. etc.

## A process <term>gradatio</term> to redden Gold <term>Solem</term> alone according to Francois de Praga

Take 16 loth <note>a historical German unit of weight, roughly 1/2 ounce or 15-16 grams</note> of **Antimony**, 8 loth of **Armenian Bole** <term>Boli Armeni</term> <note>a reddish medicinal earth or clay</note>, 5 loth of **Saltpeter** <term>Sal Nitri</term>, 1 loth of **Alum** <term>Alumen</term>, 2 loth of **Sal Ammoniac** <term>Salis Ammoniaci</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>. Crush these substances <term>Species</term> very fine. Afterwards, take 2 pounds of **Roman Vitriol** <note>copper sulfate</note>, 2 loth of common or white flour, and 4 loth of **Calcined Alum** <note>alum that has been heated to a white powder</note>. Crush these all at once and pour them together into an open **Crucible** <term>Tigell</term> and pour wine over them, so that they **dissolve** <term>solviren</term> over a short fire. And when it holds together moderately <note>original: "moderato"</note>, stir in the aforementioned powders—stirring constantly and mixing them without ceasing—until they reach 16 loth, so that they dry out completely and become as hard as a stone. Afterwards, grind the stone or the burnt-out powders fine again, and keep the powder until you need it. Then take 5 pounds and 1 loth of **Saltpeter**, 8 loth of **Vitriol**, crush them fine and pour wine over them. Place it over a small or gentle fire, stirring until it turns entirely to water. When it has cooled or chilled, **distill** it through a **Filter** <term>Filtrum</term> into a glass vessel and keep it; this shall be called **Vitriol water**.

<meta>Catchword: called</meta>

<column-break/>

When you then wish to **refine gold** <term>Aurum cementiren</term> <note>cementation was a process of heating gold with dry chemicals to remove impurities</note>, moisten or dampen the three aforementioned powders with this **Vitriol water**, and then **layer** <term>stratificire</term> them in a crucible. Once you have done this, seal or close the crucible well, and give it first a gentle fire. Afterwards, strengthen or increase the heat so that the **material** <term>Materia</term> in the crucible becomes glowing hot; let it stay in this glow for one hour, or 8 to 10 hours. However, you should be careful not to give it too harsh a fire, lest the salt flow due to excessive heat and glow; for if you see that happen, then all effort and labor is in vain and useless. If the color of the gold, as it now appears, does not yet seem red enough to you, put it back in a second time and do as before until the color pleases you. This much Francois de Praga writes of this.

### Concerning the Spirit of Eggs

Take **quicklime** <term>Calcem Vivum: a caustic substance produced by heating calcium-rich materials like eggshells or limestone</term> made from eggs, white **marble stone** <term>Marmelstein: marble, used here as another source of calcium carbonate</term>, common **salt**, crushed glass, and just as much of **purified mercury** <term>Mercurio mundo: "clean" or "purified" mercury</term>. Grind all of this **material** <term>Materia</term> seven times upon a stone, and add to it a little **mercury** and **vinegar**, so that it is <unclear>prepared</unclear> into light feathers. Gradually add **mercury** to it until it is completely **turned into a paste** <term>impastirt</term>. Afterward, grind or pound it very well, and dry it off again, and afterward grind it once more and dry it again; do this for a third and fourth time. Then **sublime** <term>sublimir: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify it</term> it in a long-necked or thin vessel, so it will become living **purified mercury** <note>original: "m. do." abbreviation for "mundo."</note> but will rise upward.

Also take one pound of this **mercury**, two pounds of **vitriol** <term>Vitrioli: metallic sulfates, often used to help the mercury sublime</term>, and also one pound of **common salt** <note>original: "Wegmehl-Salts." Then **sublime** it as before, so it will become very white and rise upward. Afterward, take a portion of this **mercury** and grind it very well upon a stone, and **imbibe** or moisten it with a little clear water until it begins to take effect and change color together.

## How one should fix Arsenic.

**Take** <term>℞: Recipe</term> 1 part Quicklime <note>calcium oxide</note> + ½ part Potash <term>Cinerum clavellatorum: literally "ash from small clubs/logs," meaning potash</term>, which is potash or sifted ash. # ### Fixation.

Likewise note / When the Stone has become volatile <term>volatilis</term> <note>capable of evaporating or rising when heated</note> and you wish to fix it entirely <note>"Fixation" is the process of making a substance stable so it no longer evaporates under heat</note>, take of the **volatile Stone**, as much as you think is enough, and place it in cucurbits <term>Cúcúrbitis</term> <note>gourd-shaped glass vessels used for distillation</note> or glass molds designed for this purpose with lids that are useful for reverberation <term>Reuerberation</term> <note>a method where heat is reflected off the top of a furnace back onto the material</note>. Give it initially a gentle **candle-fire** <term>Ignem candelæ</term> <note>a very low, steady heat like that of a single candle</note> until it no longer ascends or rises further by this light. Afterward, give it the same **candle-fire**—that is, a fire from wax or candles and lights—but one that is stronger than the previous one, which can more easily melt the paste. For this, you should use coarse paper laid three or four-fold upon one another. You can also, if you wish, place a grate before it when you want to strengthen the fire for the third time; the fire must become stronger and stronger **by degrees** <term>per gradus</term> until it finally reaches a flame or a great glowing heat. Further note also that the fixed stone should properly be dissolved / when the fixed stone absorbs <note>original: "imbibirt"</note> the **Mercury** <term>Mercuriúm</term> and is in turn absorbed by it; in such a way that if another substance were added, it would all be pure Mercury. And then that which is fixed is properly called **dissolved** <term>solútū</term> and **fusible** <term>fúsibile</term> <note>capable of being melted</note>, just as Mercury is wont to be.

How are all precious stones polished and tinted? --- Answer: When you wish to polish these same precious stones, take the stone called <term>Emery</term> <note>original: "Smerillūm"; a very hard rock used as an abrasive</note>, and pound it very fine through a skin <note>used as a sieve</note>, and clean it with **straw** <note>original: "Cūm Stramino"; possibly used to filter or brush the dust</note>. It is evident that the ore or stone was initially water, just as all **metals** <note>original: "Metalla"</note> are converted or transformed into **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note>. And briefly to say, just as every thing is generated and preserved in its own **species**—that is, its kind and genus—so also can every metal increase its **mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the "seed" or metallic soul that allows for growth</note> within its own kind. However, all **metals** are generated in the furnace and take their increase or grow through internal operations; thus, it is not impossible that **metals** may be increased and **multiplied** a countless many times. 

But such a thing cannot happen otherwise than through that which is the most perfect in their **generation** <note>birth or production</note>, namely the **matter** by which the **Elixir of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Elixir philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of perfecting base metals</note> is made **complete** and perfected. One cannot, however, arrive at this **Elixir** except through a proper middle-ground, for there is no **motion** or movement from one **extreme** <note>original: "Extremi"</note> to the other without a **medium** <note>a middle substance</note> being present; hence it is also the nature and property of the **medium** that it holds the **extremes** together.

The **extremes** <note>original: "Extrema"; referring to the two opposing poles of alchemical substance</note>, however, are **sulfur** and **mercury** <note>original: "Schwefel und Mercurius"</note>. These are not of my own invention, but rather it is the **elixir** <note>original: "Elixir"</note> which is the **completion** <note>original: "Complementum"</note>. Their **intermediaries** <note>original: "Media"</note>, however, which by nature are more inclined toward it, are transformed, **decocted** <note>original: "decoquirt"; a process of heating or boiling to extract essence</note>, and refined; they belong to the state of perfection and to us. Therefore, my dear son, let no effort or labor discourage you. For what a man asks for, that He [God] promises to you in His own time. For this reason, satisfy yourself well as to what kind of **stone** this may be for you, and of what **matter** <note>original: "Materia"</note> it is made, seeing as nothing else is added to it, except that the superfluous matter is separated or removed from it. I have also indicated that the **mastery** <note>original: "Magisterium"; the Great Work of alchemy</note> or work should be rightly understood, at which the **philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophi"</note> marvel.

Now I will further proceed to the **practice** <note>original: "Practiciren"; moving from theory to the actual laboratory work</note> with Divine help and grace, and perform the same. Therefore, take good heed of my works and my speech, and guard yourselves against folly, or the common way, and against thieves. For it is quite certain that everything that is buried in the earth does not become alive and generate its own kind until it has first died, rotted, or been destroyed.

# Follows after the Treatise of the Four Spirits: How the Bodies Should be Prepared

Since it is now necessary that one can prepare the <term>Bodies</term> <note>original: "Corpora," the alchemical term for the seven base and noble metals</note> in four different ways:

<gloss>Mercury <note>original: the symbol ☿</note></gloss> The first way belonging to the preparation is the <term>Calcination</term> <note>original: "Calcinatio," the process of reducing a metal to a powder or "lime" through high heat</note> of the bodies; that is, that one turns them into a lime. 

The second way is the <term>Ceration</term> <note>original: "Ceratio," a process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency, often by adding liquid</note> of the bodies; that is, that one grinds and <term>imbibes</term> <note>moistens or soaks</note> them upon a stone, so that their parts or portions are made fine and subtle, and thus become more suitable for <term>Solution</term> <note>original: "Solution," the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note>. 

The third way necessary in the preparation of the bodies is that one **solves** <note>dissolves</note> them in water. 

The fourth and final way is this: that one may recognize the result in a stone or a **druse** <note>original: "drüße," a cavity in a rock lined with crystals</note>. For whoever does not know the process to prepare the bodies wanders like a blind man from the path. Just as an arrow cannot reach the set target if the bow has no string, so too can no laborer bring his work to a happy and desired end unless he wisely observes and carries out these four **methods** <note>original: "Modos"</note> to prepare the bodies.

# On Arsenic

**NOTE**, that in this particular way, there will be a type of **Sulfur** <term>Sulfur; often representing the principle of combustion and soul in alchemy</term> of which the greater part is taken into the solution; for this reason, it retains no stable substance within itself, as that substance is shown and given up within it. This is a mixture where the Sulfur is more like a coagulation <note>the process of a liquid becoming solid</note> than the **Arsenic**, yet the Arsenic remains longer in the fire than the Sulfur.

# How Sulfur is Prepared

To do this, use **Distilled Atramentum** <term>Atramentum; a term for vitriol or metallic inks, usually green or blue vitriol (ferrous or copper sulfate)</term> to soak it, and then distill it. Pour the distilled water back over it again, and so it will become white and as pure as a fly <note>original: "flig-weisß", likely meaning as white as a wing or a very bright white</note>. If you perform this operation one after the other, it will be confirmed and made more powerful, as I have said. Likewise, mix **Salt** and **Honey** together and let them boil together over a gentle fire; if it is multiplied or increased, its stability shall be drawn out and taken with it. It will be yielded up by the fire. When this is done often, the Sulfur becomes beautiful, clear, and white.

# How the Stones should be Prepared

Take together **Stones of Boys** <note>original: "Stein von Knaben", a common alchemical code for the urine of young boys (urina puerorum), traditionally collected in the spring and used for its high ammonia and salt content</note> in the spring; put them into a glass or glazed vessel. <meta>This page continues the technical instructions for chemical distillation and the stabilization of substances, following the previous discussion on preparing salts and tinctures. It shifts from specific recipes to a more general classification of laboratory methods.</meta>

# On the various ways or
# methods one is accustomed to distilling waters

Note that there are three ways or methods used for the distillation of waters. The first **distillation** <note>original: "distillatio"</note> is performed by means of the **alembic** <term>Alambick; a classic alchemical still consisting of a boiling vessel and a cooling cap with a snout</term>. This is done using the best and most distinguished [vessels]. The second **distillation** is performed by means of a **filter** <term>Filtrum; often a piece of felt or cloth used to strain liquids</term>. The third is performed through sand, just like lyes.

The first distillation, using an **alembic**, is undertaken for this reason: so that the waters and **oils** <term>Olea</term> are all the more purified and improved by the rising vapor, and are clarified from harmful and vaporous materials and from **decay** <note>original: "putrefaction"</note>, so that they do not easily rot thereafter. Additionally, regarding **Sal Ammoniac** <term>Sale Armoniaco; ammonium chloride, a volatile salt central to alchemical work</term>, one should distill its water once more through an **alembic** and then **coagulate** <note>original: "coagulirt"; to thicken a liquid into a solid</note> it again, so that it is then, without any doubt, **fixed** <term>fix; stable and resistant to the heat of fire</term> and good. In no other way can **Sal Ammoniac** be fixed.

The **oil** <term>Oleum</term>, however, is distilled for this reason: so that it loses the **burning moisture** <note>original: "Adustiuam humiditatem"</note>, as I have experienced myself with **oil of bricks** <term>Oleo laterino; an oil produced by distilling bricks soaked in olive oil, used in medicine and alchemy</term>, which serves as proof of this. In the **refinement** <note>original: "rectification"</note> of the product, there is a distillation until it can no longer be burned; and the more often it is distilled, the better it will be or become, and its **tincture** <term>Tinctur; the essential color or medicinal soul of a substance</term> will also be all the better.

---

The second **distillation**, through a **filter** <term>Filtrum</term>, occurs because some raw waters, when they are dirty, cannot be purified if the **dregs** <note>original: "Faeces"</note> are not **separated** <note>original: "separirt"</note> from them. Therefore, one must use a filter so that the thick or coarse parts remain behind, and the pure part always appears beautifully clear. This is the case with **orpiment** <term>Auripigmentum; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term> and **arsenic** <term>Arsenicum</term> because of their oiliness or fattiness.

There is also another distillation that happens through sand and is very common, namely when lyes and **burnt tartar** <note>original: "Verbrenten Weinstein"</note> are distilled through sand. Note: a <unclear>brine or brew</unclear> through a **filter**.

# A good lesson or good process for
# fixation which is well worth noting

There are no **fixations** <term>Fixiones; the process of making a volatile substance stable in fire</term> better or more certain than those which are **completed** <note>original: "complet"</note> or fulfilled by the consumption [of the spirits] within the fixed **bodies** <term>Corporibus</term>. However, the **bodies** cannot become entirely clear and free until one burns the **union and communion of the bodies** <note>original: "Union communion Corpora"</note>, which is now called **incineration** <note>original: "Cineratio"</note> or **combustion** <note>original: "Combustio"</note>. This is a burning of the spirits in the fire, be it through small holes or **deflagration** <note>original: "Verpuffung"; a sudden, loud burning or small explosion</note>.

Secondly, **fixation** <term>Fixatio</term> occurs in such a way that one drives the volatile waters or moistures into the burning and yields them up. The first happens and everything is burned; let it produce as much thin or pale silver as you wish, and then a form [will emerge]...

## A Whitening <term>Dealbatio</term> from a good companion and proven friend

He took **frogspawn** <note>original: "Laich flüchlein"</note> and large **ant eggs** and **wormwood** smoke. He placed these ingredients in a new <note>original: "Unreing"; likely meaning unused</note> pile of **manure** below, and passed the box through the fire. He sealed the box with **Lute of Wisdom** <term>Luto Sapientia</term> <note>a specialized airtight clay sealant used by alchemists</note> and burned it in the **crucible** <note>original: "Schulte"</note>. He placed the crucible upon cast or molten **lead** <term>Saturnum</term> and mixed them well together. Thus, he obtained **Silver** <term>Lūnam</term>, which passed three tests.

## Another Whitening <term>Dealbatio</term> of the same good friend

He took **pigeon dung** and **litharge** <note>original: "Litargirium"; lead monoxide</note> or **silver dross**. He burned these in a new, unused box until they became powder. He placed this powder over or upon **lead** <term>Saturnum</term>. It became to him as if it were **Silver** <term>Lūna</term>; he said it had passed two tests

<column-break/>

and was like a jewel of **golden ore**. This must be **tested** <note>original: "probariert"</note> with **lead** <term>Saturnus</term> in this way: He took as much lead as he wanted and marked it. Afterward, he threw it into salt water and used the boxes frequently. Then he treated it with a little **sal ammoniac** <term>Sal Armoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note>. He said the lead had become as white to him as **silver** <term>Lūna</term>.

# Saffron of Mars <note>original: "Crocus Martis"; a term for iron oxide (rust) used in medicine and alchemy</note>
Take 1 lot of purified iron filings, and incorporate it with 1/2 lot of crystalline salt, vitriol, sweet and burnt or prepared alabaster, and let it carefully be stirred and drawn out in the heat of the sun or in a warm oven.

# How one should make burning water
Take 1 pound of tart old red wine, three years old, or 1 quintlein of arsenic, sulfur, and a half pound of mummy <note>original: "mummdie"; likely 'mumia,' a substance used in historical medicine often derived from bitumen or preserved remains</note> as the base. Put all of this into a vessel once you have mixed it, and distill it like rose water. The special properties or virtues of this water are: if you dip a finger into it and it appears to be burning, it will not actually be burnt, and you will feel no pain, unlike with a real fire. If you dip a candle into it and touch it, the water burns, yet it is not extinguished.

# To make an oil which burns and yet does no harm
Take 1 pound of turpentine, 4 parts or 1 pound of oil, with 1 pound of common salt. Distill these three in a glass flask or alembic that is well-sealed. When you wish to "burn" yourself, make a woolen cloth wet or damp with this same substance; and when you have applied it, coat it with the aforementioned oil and light it; it burns, yet it does not consume, like the light that is ignited on a table.

# To note how one should make a French Soap or Lye
<margin>which others also do</margin>
A French Soap <term>Sapo; soap</term> is made thus: One takes a "capital" <note>likely referring to a concentrated lye or "first-run" extraction</note> of either willow ash or potash <note>original: "Straschischer"; likely 'Strassburger' ash or a specific type of wood ash</note> that is finely crushed, and let that be in the third part of bird-dropping leaves <note>original: "Vogelgeschrit laubs"; potentially a specific botanical or organic additive</note>. Let a third part boil down, and then strain it off. Place bear suet <note>original: "Börin Unschalts"</note> into it, and let it boil down again so that it becomes thick. Then add a little flour to it, and let it melt down or boil again.

# To make a Roman Soap or Lye
This is made as described above, but use for the thick contents a little olive oil and "sugar-leaf" <note>original: "Sücrit Blett"; possibly a reference to a sweet herb or stevia-like plant</note>. Let it boil until it becomes thick and hard. One tests it all; if one sees it coagulate on wood, it is ready.

# Notes

The three kinds of Mercury / One is called Passive, the other Active. Passive, or common Mercury, is that which is not fully purified or "mured" <note>likely meaning matured or fixed</note>, and is prepared only to a certain extent, and is not fixed <note>stable or resistant to heat</note>. In the other kind, however, namely Active Mercury, which is also called the Mercury of the Philosophers, and is extracted or drawn out from a perfect body <note>referring to noble metals like gold or silver</note>, it is fixed / which fixes and coagulates the other, namely the passive Mercury, upon achieving coagulation. A certain measure and weight of it is taken, but one can do this many more times if one lets it drop down drop by drop / as long as it can remain powerful. ### A water that dissolves all metals.

Take 1 ounce of sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> and 1/2 pound of saltpeter. If you wish to add to this: alkali salt, prepared salt gum, euphorbium <note>the resinous sap of the spurge plant</note>, cinnabar, and saxifrage <note>a plant whose name literally means "stone-breaker"</note>

Take 1/2 pound of Roman vitriol <note>copper sulfate</note> and 1 pound of alum or "salty alum." ### A water which gives weight

Take 1 pound of litharge <note>original: Silberglett; lead oxide, a byproduct of silver refining</note>, pulverize it very finely and subtly, and sieve it through a linen cloth. Afterward, wash it in common salt water. Everything that stays on top, let it rest or stir it with a wooden spatula until it has reduced by half. Then strain it through a filter and distill it, and keep the water in a glazed ampoule. If you wish to make a "body" <note>a metal</note> more "milder" <note>softer or more malleable</note>, place it into the said water. Take it out again and let it dry; it will have gained weight.

### Regarding the fixation of sal ammoniac, a good friend says:

When its water has been distilled once more through the alembic and has coagulated again, then it is "fixed" <note>made stable or non-volatile under heat</note>. He says that this is, without any doubt, everything that it was not before; just as we gave mention above in the "Practica" <note>a section of the manuscript focused on practical laboratory work</note>.

## How one should mollify or soften iron or steel
Take hemp seeds, crush them, and take two measures of the juice. Add to it 1 measure of alkali salt <term>Salis Alkali; a basic salt often derived from plant ashes</term> and one measure of the juice of *Salatrum* <note>original: Succo Salatri; likely refers to the juice of wild lettuce or a similar plant used as a chemical agent</note>. Mix these together. In this ointment, quench or temper the material [the iron or steel] as often as you wish.

## For silver-plated vessels
Take pale and burnt... <note>The text here is somewhat obscured: "nitt Sulz thun der Schamball"</note> in a box. Moisten it with pure vinegar. And whatever vessel you smear with it and then dry again by the fire, that same piece will become like silver <note>original: lüna; the alchemical term for silver, named for the Moon</note>, and it will remain so forever and ever.

## To make a very beautiful and magnificent blue color
Take copper <note>original: Venerem; the alchemical term for copper</note> and calcine it into a powder. Afterward, place another box [or crucible] in a furnace, but in such a way that the fire is behind it, surrounding the box. The box, however, should lie on its side in the furnace, and its hole or opening should protrude out of the furnace. It should be fixed all around within the furnace with lute <note>symbol: $\ddagger$; a specialized alchemical clay used to seal vessels</note>. Place the aforementioned lime [powdered copper] inside and continue the burning for three days without ceasing until the color pleases you. Examine the powder by taking a little bit out and on...
<meta>catchword: take</meta>

<column-break/>

take, or test it with lead <note>symbol: $\hbar$</note> and vitriol <note>symbol: $\ominus$; a sulfate mineral</note>. For you should test these spirits <note>volatile alchemical substances</note> on a "milt" <note>likely a test plate or a soft metallic surface</note>; then hang them in a pale, glazed tile in a box, as you well know.

## Testing Gold <note>symbol: $\odot$</note>
Take silver <note>original: Luna</note> 2 parts, gold <note>original: solis / $\odot$</note> 1 part, and vitriol <note>symbol: $\ominus$</note> and lute <note>symbol: $\ddagger$</note>. Rub the lute upon the "belly" [the curved side of the crucible]. Place it in a crucible, and when you have it in flux, then throw upon it the vitriol and lute. Place one piece after another in several parts; ensure that you mix it with a piece of hazel wood. After the successive projections <note>the act of throwing a substance onto a molten metal to transform it</note>, apply it also to the plates on the glass. After it has been made well-glowing, let it be quenched; then throw it into oil of vitriol <note>original: Oleum $\ominus$</note> and lute. Then it will "desire the fire" and become bold [dense and vibrant]. This holds firm even if one makes it red-hot. But it suffers nothing even if one should want to cast or melt it. In *peranzone* <note>likely a specific refining vessel or a corruption of the term for a cupel</note> it also holds firm without an examination of calcination, which has changed the color (according to Bernhard <note>likely Bernhardus Trevisanus, a famous 15th-century alchemist</note> or common lute). Thus it tinctures more or less. Praise and thanks be to God the Lord for it; thus far and so.

# NOTE ON WEIGHTS <note>original: "NOTA DE PONDERIBVS"</note>, that is
## The names of weights, and what each contains

<margin>1</margin> Six ounces weigh 12 Lot <term>Lot; a traditional German unit of weight, usually 1/32 of a pound</term>, which make one Mark <term>Mark; a weight used for gold and silver, roughly 233 grams</term>.
<margin>2</margin> Three ounces weigh 6 Lot.
<margin>3</margin> Twelve ounces or 24 Lot make two Marks.
<margin>4</margin> One Pound <note>original: "Libra"</note> or Pfundt contains two Marks.
<margin>5</margin> A Hemina <note>original: "Hemina"; an ancient measure of volume, here being equated to weight</note>, as it is read by those in the household; it contains,
for certain, one ounce or 2 Lot; see better info above <note>original: "vide supra melius"</note>.
<margin>6</margin> A Scruple <note>symbol: ℈</note> signifies the ninth part
of a Drachma <term>Drachma; also known as a Dram</term> or Quintlein.
<margin>7</margin> A Drachma <note>symbol: ʒ</note> signifies the ninth
part of an ounce.
<margin>8</margin> An Ounce <note>original: "Vncia"</note>, one ounce or 2 Lot <insert>}</insert> is the eighth
part of a Mark.
<margin>9</margin> Twenty grains of wheat <note>original: "Viginti grana tritici"</note> make or contain one scruple.
<margin>10</margin> Three scruples <note>original: "Tres scrupuli"</note> contain
one Drachma or Quintlein.
<margin>11</margin> Eight Drachmas or eight Dram-weights contain one
ounce or 2 Lot.
<margin>12</margin> Twelve ounces or 24 Lot
make the standard pound; or for us,
it contains 16 ounces or 32 Lot.

<column-break/>

<margin>13</margin> Two and a half pounds <note>original: "Duæ libræ cum semisse"</note> make one
sextarium <term>Sextarium; a Roman measure of volume, roughly a pint</term> or small measure.
<margin>14</margin> Take four times five scruples for the weight of a drachma <note>original: "Dragmæ quater quinque scripulum pro pondere sume"</note>.
<margin>15</margin> In a drachma, the scruple rises multiplied by three <note>original: "In drachma scripulis ter surgit multiplicatus"</note>;
that is, one scruple multiplied with
another gives three times that.
<margin>16</margin> A Mark <note>original: "Marca"</note> is 1/2 pound. One Mark contains half
a pound, weighing four ounces, which is three Lot <note>note: the math here varies by regional standards</note>.
<margin>17</margin> A Drachma is one *Quintinus* <note>Dram</note>, which is worth
as much as a fourth part of a Lot. That is, a Drachma
is the same as a Quintlein, and is worth
the 4th part of a Lot.
<margin>18</margin> A Scruple <note>original: "Scrupulus"</note> is the fourth part of a Quintlein.

### How one should prepare Cerussa or White Lead

Take a strong vinegar or wine vinegar and fill a vessel halfway with sharp wine vinegar. Then place very thinly hammered lead sheets inside, ensuring that they do not touch the vinegar. Then seal the pot with a brick coated in clay so that no air or moisture can mix with it. When the pot is well-secured so that no smoke or vapor can escape, place it under the earth and surround the pot with horse manure <note>the fermentation of horse manure was a standard alchemical method for providing a gentle, consistent "wet" heat</note>.

<column-break/>

Sink it down or around and let it stand there for a month. When you later take the pot out, you will find white lead sheets. Scrape off the white substance clinging to the sheets with a small knife or steel tool. Afterward, place the pot back into the earth as before. If you wish to have more, add more small sheets in the same order as previously described, and everything will be collected again into a white substance from the lead. It is thick and is called **Spanish White** <note>original: "Album de Hispania"</note>. (Do not use tin sheets instead of the small lead sheets; this must be done according to the exact order as shown for the white substance of lead). A similar thing is also made into **Spanish White Lead** <note>likely referring to Verdigris, though the text calls it white lead</note> if one takes copper sheets instead of the small lead sheets and works them through the same painted method; however, ensure the sheets do not touch the **vinegar** <note>original: "Acetum"</note> by placing supports in the pot above the vinegar, and then placing the sheets upon them as we have taught you.

->Thanks be to God<-

### An Augmentation or Addition for White

Heat **Quicksilver** <term>Mercurium; the metal Mercury</term> in a shard or earthenware vessel until it begins to smoke. Then add subtle silver leaf, which has been previously anointed or smeared with **Hezo** or **feather-alum water** <note>likely a solution of alum or a specific mineral water</note> and also heated until it melts.

In the stream, dissolve or quench it gently again, and take everything that is the "flower" <note>the fine powdery residue or oxidation</note> from the zinc itself. ### How one should prepare a precious Red Tincture

Take 1 part of **mineral calx** <note>original: "de Calcesturi," likely referring to a metallic oxide or dross</note> that has been gently burned and calcined. Dissolve it in two parts of sal ammoniac water. Then set this same calx aside with the mixed water until it has dried very gently. Then put it into a sealed glass and set it for eight days in a damp place, and it will dissolve into a **red water** which then remains like glass.

With this water, afterward treat **sublimated mercury** until you have soaked it seven times, drying it out each time, and also letting it sit until it becomes very red. Afterward, grind it once more with sal ammoniac water and place it in a damp place; it will be dissolved into a water. Thereafter, place this same water in a warm oven for half a day, and it will become a **red coagulated powder** like **Cinnabar** <note>original: "Zinober," a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide</note>. Cast 1 part of this powder over one hundred parts of **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> and melt it into a mass. It will become a pure and clear **Gold** <note>original: "Sol," the planetary name for gold</note>, most powerful and permanently stable or enduring. However, how you should calcine the Gold <note>original: "Solem"</note> was taught above.

## according to our John is as follows:

He took stones from Teuren <note>likely a specific geological location or type of stone</note> which he ground, and he burned them at the same time, just as **tartar** <term>Tartarum; the sediment from wine casks</term> or **cream of tartar** <note>original: "Weinstain"</note> is usually **combusted** <note>original: "conburirt"</note>. He did this so that they became quite white, even if they had still been black on the inside, as usually happens. After that, he crushed them into small pieces and passed them through a sieve. These pieces he burned well, like tartar, in a **brick kiln** <note>original: "Ziegelofen"</note> or in a **potter’s kiln** <note>original: "Haffners Ofen"</note>, which he preferred; thus he gave it a good fire so that the material became quite white.

When the same material had cooled, he added to it a half-part of pure white [substance] and made it into a **paste** <note>original: "pasten"</note> by pressing or kneading it together with his hands. Thereafter, he formed it, perhaps in a copper or wooden mold, into the shape of a **solid crucible** <term>Tigel; a heat-resistant container for melting metals or minerals</term>. He let it dry thoroughly and kept it for his work whenever it was needed. When he had made this according to the first preparation, he then **processed** <note>original: "laborirt"</note> it a second, third, and fourth time; thus the crucible became so strong that it could withstand the fire and remain stable very well. ### Make Another Lute
<note>Lute (from the Latin "lutum," meaning clay or mud) was a heat-resistant paste used by early chemists and alchemists to seal joints in distillation apparatus or to "loricate" (coat) glass vessels so they wouldn't shatter in high heat.</note>

Take slaked lime or **potter’s clay** <term>Letten; a heavy, sticky clay used as a base for heat-resistant mixtures</term> and temper it with warm water, **pounding it well** <note>original Latin: "bene maleando"</note>. Add small stones and pit-sand, as is the custom in the Luten region or Bohemia. Then take horse manure that is not too old, and shavings from a trough, such that the shavings make up a fourth part and the clay makes up a third part. Mix and beat them together well, and let them **ferment or rot** <term>Compustriren; the practice of allowing organic matter in clay to decay, which improved the lute's plasticity and binding strength</term> for a time. Afterward, temper them with hot water and coat the glass with the mixture.

### How One Should Prepare Lead
<note>The author uses the alchemical name "Saturnum" (Saturn) for lead.</note>

Take a new **pot** <term>Haften; a ceramic crucible or melting pot</term> and place it in a furnace. Put into it **lead** <term>Saturnum</term> and **tin** that have never been used before, so that the lead melts. When it is melted, stir it back and forth with an iron spatula until it burns away into a powder and becomes a light or lemon-colored powder <note>This process describes the creation of litharge (lead oxide), a yellow powder used in glass-making and assaying.</note>. Afterward, grind the same powder very finely and pour water over it. Stir it very strongly with a wooden spatula until the water becomes quite cloudy. Then pour that same cloudy water into another vessel, and pour more water over the residue again, stirring it strongly as before. When this is done, pour it off again and add it to the first water. Continue this until you have drawn all the fine material out of the **dregs** <note>original: "facibus"; the solid residue</note>. The coarse dregs that remain at the bottom, **calcine** <term>calcinire; to roast a substance at high heat until it oxidizes and crumbles into powder</term> them again in a pot as before. Then separate the fine from the coarse, and calcine the coarse dregs again until they become small and fine.

# How one shall calcine gold finely and with little effort
<note>Calcination is the process of heating a metal in air until it turns into a fine powder (an oxide), making it "open" for further chemical work.</note>

Take pure gold and make an amalgam <term>Amalgama; a mixture of gold and mercury</term>. When you have added three parts [of salt] to the amalgam, mix it with common salt and sublime the mercury <note>the process of heating the mixture so the mercury turns to vapor and rises, leaving the gold behind</note> away from the salt. Afterward, separate the common salt from the body <note>the gold residue</note> with warm water, and wash it with fresh water. Thus you will find a light or very precious calx <note>the fine gold powder left after calcination</note>.

# An Extract or Selection from the *Satyrennensian Book*, which is titled *The Direct Path, Chapter [blank]*

The practitioners and masters of **alchemy** <term>alchimia</term> cannot do without or lack a furnace. Therefore, these furnaces should be constructed and understood according to the quantity and scale of the operation. Whatever materials are to be processed there must be sufficient, and if the work is primarily large-scale, the furnace must also be built and prepared proportionately larger. If, however, the work is slight and small, then the furnaces must also be sized according to the quantity or mass of the things and materials. For this reason, I will provide here an instruction and teaching that shall be useful and beneficial to both parties. But first, I will speak of the **Philosophical Furnace** <term>Furnello Philosophico</term> and how it should be prepared and built.

First, this furnace should be placed not far from a wall, so that the wind may reach it all the better and more easily. However, it should stand one arm’s length away from the wall. At the bottom, a pit shall be made, one ell deep and two spans wide, or a little wider. And this structure should be plastered with the **Lute of the Mastery** <term>Luto Magisterij</term>. Around this pit, a wall shall be built of brick or clay, which appears to serve as a column, and it should be two feet and one span thick; then let it dry out.

Next, you must have a grate <note>original: "Ratt," literally a wheel; here referring to a circular furnace grate</note> made of the very best potter's clay <term>Haffner letten; high-quality clay used by potters to withstand intense heat</term> or loam, which can withstand [the heat] in every respect. ### Here begins a good and precious Whitening

<term>Deallatio; dealbation, the alchemical process of whitening or purifying a substance to prepare it for further transmutation.</term>

Take 1 part of crystalline sublimated **Arsenic**, 1 part of calcined **Tartar** <term>Tartari; Cream of Tartar or potassium bitartrate, often used as a flux</term>. Take about 32 parts <note>original symbols: $\text{\textrecipe}$ $z$ 911 . 32.</note>, almost as much. Mix the Arsenic with the 32 parts of the material, and mix them into one another. And if the **White Stone** <note>original: *Weistein*; refers to Tartar or "potash"</note> is to go into a pot, then imbibe those powders—namely the Arsenic and the Tartar—with the **Oil** <term>Oleo; likely a chemical oil or "Oil of Tartar"</term> upon a marble stone. If, however, no oil is available, then mix a very little bit of the Tartar finely over the other halves, and imbibe them and drive them with **Water of Life** <term>Aqua Vite; concentrated distilled alcohol</term>, with wine or vinegar, or also with an agitator, until it becomes like a sludge or mud-like paste. 

Then lay the prepared material into a glazed **distilling vessel** <note>original: *deistellin*; likely an aludel or specialized ceramic dish</note>, and set it to a fire; clean it and place upon the distilling vessel

Afterward take it out, and that which has been calcined—which will be a small amount—because it must be processed once more with **Water of Life** and sugar and drugged <note>original: *drogieret*; likely meaning treated with further medicinal or chemical additives</note> for a short time, and once more with sugar day and night, but always with a gentle fire, as small as you can have it at the start. # A small method <term>vía</term> for Arsenic <term>Arsenici</term>

Take 1 lb of well-pulverized **Arsenic**, and take with it 2 lb of copper filings. Place them in a vessel and let them boil <note>In alchemy, "boiling" or "seething" often refers to long-term digestion at a steady heat.</note> for three weeks until the mixture becomes completely black. Afterward, dry it thoroughly in an earthen **Sublimation vessel** <term>Sublimatorio</term> that is glazed on the inside. Take great care with these **earthen instruments** which have been glazed inside. First, create a gentle fire beneath it until the moisture has been drawn out. Then, strengthen the fire, and the substance will rise very high to the top. You do not need to examine it further.

# A small sublimation <term>sublimatio</term> of Sal Ammoniac <term>Salis Armoniaci</term>

Take again 1 lb of well-pulverized **Sal Ammoniac** and 1 lb of **Crystal Salt** <note>likely purified rock salt or sea salt</note>. Pulverize them well and place this powder into an earthen vessel. Let it boil and boil in **Vinegar** <term>Essigh</term> three times; then let it dry out. Place it upon or into a **sublimation vessel** <term>sublimatorium</term> as described in the other or previous instructions. There, it will become a good **sublimate**, which can be prepared in a single day.

A **sublimation** of **Sulphur** <term>Sulphuris</term> is useful; however, the **Sulphur** is **whitened** <term>dealbirt</term> or made white over two months, provided it is kept among the pits or fumes <note>The original "gräuben oder qvualen" likely refers to the digestion process in a heat-pit or the fuming of the substance</note> with **Urine** <term>Harn</term> and **better Vinegar** every day. And when it has become dry, dry it again. In this way, it will become as beautiful, bright, and white as snow.

# The Universal Way through the Grinding of Mars
<note>Latin: *Via Universalis per Contritionem martis*. While "Mars" traditionally refers to iron, the recipe here calls for silver; "Contrition" refers to the literal grinding or "mortification" of the metal.</note>
## Of Mars

In the Name of God the Most High
Take 1 Mark <note>A unit of weight, roughly 230 grams</note> of the very finest **Silver**, and file it down to the smallest pieces. And take 3 Marks of **Salmiac** <term>⚹</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note> which has been well sublimated; the whiter it is, the better it serves the Work. Take 1 Mark of **Sublimated Sulfur**, as white as the former, and 1 Mark of the **Eagle** <note>Latin: *Aquila*; a name for sal ammoniac or a mercurial sublimate</note> or **Mercury** <term>☿</term> which should also be well sublimated. Grind all of these together upon a stone. And see to it that when you sublimate the **Mercury**, you must always catch its moisture or humidity. Take 1 part [of the powder], and 1 part of **Spirit of Wine** <note>Latin: *Aqua Vitæ*</note> that has been distilled eight times. With these, imbibe <note>Soak or saturate</note> the aforementioned material for a full day and night, in such a way that you soften it strongly so it becomes a paste that is not too soggy. Put this material into a glass and sublimate it over a gentle fire until the moisture can pass out through the helm <note>The top part of the still</note> above; thereafter, increase [the heat]. After this, take the material out, crush or grind it, and add to it the mentioned water. Repeat this three times: namely, sublimating, grinding, and imbibing with the mentioned water.
<meta>catchword: As then</meta>

<column-break/>

As then, take the material out again and grind it upon a stone, and set it in a damp place or in a cellar. There, the material will dissolve into liquid. This dissolved "water" should be reduced or brought back again upon a stone into a material that is not dissolved, and grind it so that it may dissolve all the sooner. And when the material will no longer dissolve, put it into a glass and pour over it the water that had previously dissolved. Set a **blind helm** <note>A still-cap without a spout, used for circulation rather than collection</note> over it, and let it dry in the ashes <note>An ash-bath for even heating</note> over a gentle fire, so that the material is better digested or refined by the constant rising and falling of the vapor. Coagulate it until it becomes dry, and maintain this process, setting it intensely. Afterward, take it out again and grind it, and proceed in all steps as I have recently set down: namely, with sublimating, with the escape of moisture, and with imbibing that same moisture. Repeat this [three] times. See to it also that you govern the fire yourself, so that it is increased steadily by degrees. Finally, take the material out and dissolve it upon a stone as stated, and then it will be sounder and easier to dissolve into a water than it was before.

or along with their waters. And when it has been

and dissolved therewith, it is then
called an **Everlasting Water** <term>Aqua perennis</term>. And this water
essentially transforms all spirits into itself.
The other kind—namely the **sophistical Solidification**—
happens along with impure **bodies**
and **spirits**. Thus, the
bodies and spirits must be purified or
refined. For the Philosophers maintain
that no impure body can be **illuminated** <note>perfected or transformed</note>
together with an impure spirit or
ghost. However, when a pure spirit is placed and
implanted into a
pure body, the body will then become
perfect.

## On the Various Fixations of Mercury

Note that there are various **fixations of Mercury** <term>Fixatio Mercurij</term> <note>the alchemical process of making a volatile substance, like mercury, solid and able to withstand fire</note>. The first occurs through manifold repetitions and **grindings** <term>contritiones</term>, until it becomes fixed. However, one should hold it for certain and know that it is fixed with its water, which is of many kinds. But the water which is called **Perennial Water** <note>original: *Aqua perennis*</note> is the best, as far as its perfection and completeness are concerned. Every water of a like body is called "Perennial Water." You may be certain of this: no **spirit** <note>a volatile substance that evaporates easily</note> can be **joined** <term>iungirt</term> unless it is first **dissolved** <term>sol-virt</term>. Thus, the water of the body is made: Take a **calcine** <note>a substance reduced to powder by heat</note> of the body which you have preferred and prepare it with **water of alkali salt** <note>original: *Aqua salis Alkali*, likely a lye or caustic solution</note>. Then lay the well-dissolved matter in a vessel suitable for solution, and when it becomes mild, you will have Perennial Water. This now fixes the spirits and **coagulates the mercury** <term>coagulirt den Mercurium</term> <note>turns the liquid metal into a solid</note>.

## To fix Mercury

Take **Gall of Nitre** <note>original: *Fellis Nitri*, a specific salt formation</note>, **Antimony Ruby** <term>Spießglasrubell</term> <note>a red glass-like substance made from antimony</note>, red **Tartar**, **Antimony** <term>Spießglas</term> or lime mixed with **Alum** <term>Alumen</term>, of each 1 part; **Salt Nitre**, **Orpiment** <term>Auripigmenti</term> <note>a yellow arsenic mineral</note>, and **Sal Ammoniac** <note>original: *salis Armoniaci*</note>, of each 1/2 **Mark** <note>a unit of weight, roughly 230 grams</note>.

<meta>catchword: These all</meta>

<column-break/>

These all shall be ground down, **decocted** <term>decquiren</term> <note>extracted by boiling</note> or allowed to boil in an **alkali lye** <term>Capitello Alkali</term> for fourteen days. Afterward, place that same **lime** <note>referring to the powdered residue</note> in a crucible secured at the bottom and **drive it** <note>subject it to high heat</note> well ten times. Make a hole with your thumb in the lime and place the previously prepared matter in the little hole. Place **coagulated Mercury** on top of it, and cover it with the aforementioned powder. Finally, place **unslaked lime** <note>original: *ungelöschten Kalck*, quicklime or calcium oxide</note> on top until the vessel is full. Then close the vessel and seal it well with the **Lute of Wisdom** <term>Luto Sapientiae</term> <note>a special airtight alchemical clay used to seal joints and vessels</note>. Set it to the fixation air or however the furnace should be.

## A Coagulation of Mercury

Take **unslaked limestone**, make a hole in it, and place Mercury in the hole. Close the hole with another unslaked limestone that has been made very level. Lay unslaked lime all around it—below, above, and on the sides—to the thickness of two fingers. Sprinkle it every day with a little wine that is three days old, and repeat the operation three or four times; thus it will become hard and beautiful enough.

In this little white book, I will tell how the earths are to be made, and how one shall extract or separate the spirits from the bodies, and how certain bodies are to be extracted or drawn out from others, which are set down here as being four spirits and seven bodies. ## How one should separate gold from silver

Take unslaked pebbles found in flowing water, and bones of animals in equal **parts** <note>original: "Ann"</note>, and burn them well beforehand in a brick kiln.

## Regarding the black vitriol

Take the black **vitriol** <term>atramentum; a term usually referring to ferrous sulfate or black metallic salts used for making ink and acids</term> and, once it is made pure, **dissolve** it first with purified **alum**, **distill** it, and **coagulate** it. Then put it into a small clamp <note>original: "klembel"; perhaps a small crucible or specialized container</note> so that all the moisture is extracted or drawn out, and the dregs <note>original: "feces"</note>, which are **calcined** <term>calcinirt; heated to a high temperature to be reduced to a powder</term> in this distillation **upon the porphyry stone** <note>original: "super Porphyrium"; a hard stone slab used by alchemists for grinding and mixing chemicals</note>, or the same are **dissolved** and **coagulated** in honor-water <note>original: "ehrwaßer"; possibly a reference to 'strong water' or aqua fortis</note>, or whatever water pleases the master, shall be preserved, etc.

# Of Vitriol

Take note: when the waters or **vitriols** <term>Vitrioll; a group of sulfate minerals, often used for making acids or inks</term> are prepared, **black vitriol** <note>original: "Atramentum Nigrum"</note> is also made. Other types of vitriols are also found, which are purified in no other way than the aforementioned methods for these vitriols.

# Of the Blood of Glass or Black Glass

Take note: the **blood of glass** <note>original: "sanguineum Vitri"; likely a reference to a red-tinted glass or a specific mineral like hematite</note> or **black glass** <note>original: "Schartz glaß"</note> must first be ground. When it is thoroughly ground, one dissolves it in common warm water. Afterward, one distills it through a **filter** <note>original: "Filtrum"</note> and lets it coagulate. Finally, it should be **calcined** <term>calciner; heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile components or reduce it to powder</term> over a gentle fire.

# Of Glacial Alum or Ice-Claw

Take note: **glacial alum** <note>original: "Alumine glaciali"</note> or **ice-claw** <note>original: "Eis Klauu"; a folk name for clear, ice-like alum crystals</note> is a substance from which many things can be made and prepared. For this substance, one does not need to make it completely pure or clean in the fire. However, if it is lacking, one may purify it thus: Take note, place it in a small cloth and draw out all of its **moisture** <note>original: "Feümeditatem"</note>. In this short time, it can be used for very many things. It shall remain at the bottom of the vessel, becoming shorter <note>likely meaning more concentrated</note> on a stone from which [the moisture] was extracted or drawn out a day before, and then it shall be kept or preserved.

### Of Melted or
### Flowed Salt

Take 1 **lot** <term>a historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce</term> of **unslaked lime** <term>Ungeleschten kalck; calcium oxide, a caustic substance used to increase the reactivity of the mixture</term> and an equal amount of **common salt** <term>Sal commune; table salt</term>. Incorporate them together on a **porphyry stone** <term>lapide Porphyrio; a hard, purple-flecked stone used by apothecaries for grinding and mixing substances</term> with common oil or linseed oil. Afterward, let it dry well; then wash it with warm water and filter it through a **filter** <note>original: "Filtrum"; usually a cloth or paper funnel used for clarification</note>. Solidify the liquid, and you will have **fixed salt** <note>original: "Salem fixum"; a salt that does not vaporize when heated</note> or the "whole" of the salt.

### How One Should Solidify Common Salt

Take our common salt and wrap it in a wet linen cloth. Place it into warm ashes and repeat this process seven times. Let it **decoct** <term>decoquieren; to boil down or concentrate a substance by heating</term> until it has become completely dry. **Anneal** <note>original: "unglude"; to heat and then cool slowly to remove internal stress</note> the glass vessel. Afterward, pull it through a filter and use it. All of this is done so that the salt is not **calcinated** <term>calcinirt; reduced to a powder by high heat</term> prematurely, because "accidental moisture" remains within it, which burns and glows in lyes and oils within a sharp **crucible** <term>Co.; likely an abbreviation for *Corpus* (body) or *Cornuta* (a retort), but here referring to the heating vessel</term>.
