# Alkali Salt in Another
->Way it can be made<-

Take unslaked <unclear>vivi</unclear> alkali lime, and lime <unclear>finely</unclear> calcined <note>original: "geglüt"</note>, and pour about one measure of water over it. Let it stand for three days, and then strain it. Then take fresh Alkali Salt and the lime, with 4 parts of the drawn-off water, and then strain it well. Place in it half as much purified and sublimated Sal Ammoniac <term>Salis Armoniaci; ammonium chloride, often used as a flux or to increase the reactivity of a solution</term>. Thus you shall have a melting-water, which in one hour vanishes or melts the lime into a <unclear>single</unclear> body <note>original: "vno Corpore"</note>.

# Alkali Salt is Thus Prepared

Take 4 pounds of potash <term>Cineris clavellati; literally "club ashes," a high-quality potassium carbonate made from hardwood ashes</term> or wine dregs, and add caustic lime <note>original: "liegend kalcks"</note>, and make a lye. Afterward, let it be drawn off through a filter. Then take 8 **loth** <term>a historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams</term> of saltpeter <note>original: "Nitri Salz"</note>, 4 **loth** of Sal Ammoniac, half a pound of well-calcined tartar <term>Weinstain; the crust from wine barrels, burned to a white ash</term>, and 8 **loth** of salmiac. Grind them all well and place them together in the prepared lye and let them **boil** <term>coquiren; to cook or digest over heat</term> for half an hour. Let it settle, then strain it through a filter. Take what was drawn off and let it boil down again until it becomes completely dry. With such alkali water <note>original: "Aqua Alkali"</note>, prepare the metal filings <note>original: "Lima turam"</note>.

# A Fixation of Silver <note>original: "Fixatio lünæ"</note> Which [is] the Silver
->from the book MAXTHP<-

Take 1 pound of common salt and 1 pound of red tartar. Crush them well together, and pour clear wine over it. Let it boil a little, then let it settle and strain it through a filter. Then take **silver plates** <term>lünam laminatam; silver beaten into thin sheets to increase its surface area for chemical reaction</term> and place them **layer upon layer** <term>sss.; an abbreviation for 'stratum super stratum', a common technique of layering metal and chemicals in a crucible</term>. **Cement** <term>Cementire; the process of heating a metal in contact with powdered reagents to refine it or change its properties</term> it for one hour or twelve. Afterward, melt it two or three times, or four times with the alkali salt. But the alkali salt shall always be <unclear>combined</unclear> and burned with it; even that which was silver [should be] 1 **loth**, and the alkali should also be 1 **loth**. And then **cement** it as before, and melt it also as before with alkali.

->Flux<-

# How to Harden Glass
->So that it bends rather than breaks, and<-
->can maintain its form in the fire<-

Note that those who labor or operate in this high art of Alchemy <term>Alchimia; the medieval forerunner of chemistry, focused on the transformation of matter</term> require many glass vessels for their work. However, these cannot all be made with the same craftsmanship or quality. For some glasses are quite delicate, and others are far too brittle, such that they break from mere smoke or a draft of air. This happens out of the sheer deceit of the glassmakers and for the sake of the profit they seek, namely when they do not fully purify <note>original: "purgieren"</note> the glass in their furnaces, as the masters or artists themselves admit. If you, however, wish to use glass in your work and fear for its safety, or if you want it to be strong so that it neither breaks nor shatters easily: Take horse hooves <note>original: "Caballen klawen"; from the Latin 'caballus'</note>, cut them into small pieces, and add wine <note>original: "Wein"</note> to them. Afterward, distill a water from it. Quench the glass in this water, and it will become so hard that it can no longer be smashed <note>original: "zubroschen"</note>, and it will endure very well in the fire. A man named Gregorius N. has demonstrated this and given testimony of it.

### Vitriol is thus purified according to common chemical art <note>original: "kimen"; likely a variation of "alchemia" or "chimie"</note>

### ->An Increase for Coinage, Not for Our Composition<-

### ->A Purification of Sol, which is Gold<-

### ->A Fine Rule of a Work<-

Take one part of purified **copper** <term>Veneris</term> and one part of pure gold, and melt them together. Afterward, let **plates** <note>original: "Luminas"</note> be made from them, which are made glowing hot therein, then [quench them] just now in **brick oil** <term>Ziegel Öllen: a sharp, corrosive oil made by distilling bricks soaked in olive oil</term>. Afterward, **grind** <note>original: "dweile," likely to rub or process with liquid</note> the same with **borax water** <term>Aqua Boraris: a solution of borax used as a flux</term> and with its salt, and drive them here and there. # A Good Cementation
<note>Cementation is a dry-heat process used to refine gold or change its color by layering metal sheets with powdered minerals.</note>

# On Brass [made] from Copper

Note that the luster of **Venus** <term>Venus, the alchemical name for Copper</term> or **Copper** becomes **Brass** <note>original Latin: "Aurichalcum"</note>. However, so that it might be even more similar to **Gold**, one usually adds a little **Zinc** <term>Spiaut</term>. But if one wishes to add **Orpiment** <term>Auripigmentum, a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term> or **Arsenic** to these colors—especially the unrefined kind—and mixes or tempers it in, it takes away the luster and gives it a dirty, earthy color, which makes the additions look dark or shadowy. There are, however, some who wish to make it as shiny and bright as **Gold**. They bind **Calamine** <term>Lapidem Calaminarem, a zinc ore used in brass making</term> so that it remains fixed within for a long time and does not evaporate or turn to vapor. It is bound or "ligated" <note>original: "ligirt"</note> in this way with **Oil of Vitriol** <term>Oleo Vitri, concentrated sulfuric acid</term>. One takes fragments of glass or small broken pieces of glass, grinds them into powder, and sprinkles the powder into a crucible or shard upon the ore. After the **Calamine** has been put in and the glass has melted on top of the ore or copper, it does not let the stone or the stone's power evaporate or steam away; instead, it reflects or bends and drives the vapors of the stone back into the copper.

<meta>catchword: and thus</meta>

<column-break/>

And thus the copper is etched long and strongly enough, and it is burned around in the dense matter <note>original Latin: "faculenta materia," referring to thick or dreg-filled substance</note> that is within. Finally, it evaporates through the **Oil of Vitriol**, and then the virtue or power of the stone also evaporates with it. ## A Digestion of the Sulfur

Take the oil of Roman <term>Vitriol</term> <note>sulfuric acid derived from iron or copper sulfates</note> and add to it "sulfur articularis" <note>a specific form of sulfur, possibly "joint-sulfur" used in medicine or a crystallized form</note> or sulfur made according to the Art which is quite pure. He who finds me, and having found me, loves me, would live for a thousand years, and every day he would feed a thousand people without any defect or lack. <note>This riddle-like introduction suggests the miraculous, restorative power of the "Silver" medicine, implying it functions as a form of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

After this, let it stand and cool again until the <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> settles according to the <term>Silver</term> <note>original: "Luna"</note>. Fill the mentioned flask a second time with fresh water and let it distill once more, and finally let it be done one last time when the <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "Materia"</note> has drunk everything up. Then set it—

## Another Purification of Mercury

Take 16 ounces of mineral **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> that has never been used in any other work, and press it three times through a thick linen cloth, then through a hare-skin, and for the third time through a thick cloth or Brabant linen. This must be a proper grinding; and if anything of its coarseness remains in the skin or the cloth, creating a foulness or **dregs** <note>original: "foecis"</note>, then that Mercury is not suitable for the Operation at all. However, if nothing is present or left behind, the Mercury is good. In this regard, the **philosophical purifications** <note>The "purgationes" refer to the cleansing of the "First Matter" from its earthy impurities before it can be used in the Great Work.</note> may and can be well considered here, except for those contained in the Catalog, etc.

## An Elixir Based on Realgar

Dissolve 1 ounce of good **silver** <note>original: "lúna"</note> in **strong water** <note>original: "Aqua forti"; nitric acid</note> and 1 ounce of **sublimated arsenic** <note>original: "súblimirte Arsenici"</note>; dissolve this also so that it becomes a strong water. Afterward, put both masses together—the arsenic and the silver—into a glass and let it stand for several days in warm or hot ashes so that the masses are well united with one another. # Here Follows a Small Treatise or Book on the Art of Refining
<note>original: "Brennekunst"; literally 'the art of burning,' referring to the fire-based methods of metallurgy and assaying.</note>

First, we wish to speak of the **furnace** <term>Furnello</term> <note>original: "Furnello"; the Italian or Latinized term for a furnace, often used specifically for alchemical or metallurgical ovens.</note> belonging to **cementation** <note>A process where gold is purified by heating it with granulated materials like brick dust and salts, which react with and remove impurities.</note>. When the furnace is prepared by rough labor and likewise ready, make a hole one hand wide. And make there a pit in the middle of the floor, loosened just as in no other kind of furnace. And shape the upper part nicely round in the middle of the floor, finished like a brick-work. And make a door in the furnace, as the model indicates. And set as much of that material with the **cement** <note>original: "Cemento"; the reactive powder mixture used in the purification process.</note> as you require. And block up the door of the furnace and make a fire beneath it for a day and a night. Then take it out from the floor which is hardened; it contains gold. Afterward, rub the floor and [add] a little lead, and make a **crucible** <term>Tiegell</term> out of the floor and melt it down. Only then does he have gold in the crucible; place it upon the **cupel** <term>Cineritium</term> <note>original: "Cineritium"; a shallow, porous vessel made of bone ash used in an **assay furnace** to separate precious metals from lead.</note>, that is, upon the **assay furnace** <term>probir Ofen</term>. Thus you must have gold, and as much lead as the smoke [requires]. And afterward, heat the crucible, and that which you have in the lead
<meta>catchword: or silver</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>247</page-num>
or silver toward the day [light]. And melt it through the furnace with lead; thus you shall recover your silver. Then break the **furnace** <term>Furnum</term> into small pieces and separate it in a small **separation vessel** <term>Tieblein der Separation</term> and keep the same. Then let it be made fine and put that into the lead which was in the furnace, and melt it through the **smelting furnace** <note>original: "(et confla per Furnacem)"; Latin for "and melt through the furnace."</note>. And lay it through a crucible or **hearth-bed** <term>Berst</term> <note>original: "Berst"; likely referring to the 'breast' or porous lining of a furnace used in refining.</note>. And when it has been purified through the crucible, let it flow through; so will it be pure and good.

## Concerning the Smelting Furnace of Gold and Silver
<note>original: "Furnello Conflutionis"; Latin for 'furnace of melting' or smelting furnace.</note>

Make a small furnace two or two-and-a-half hands long out of the **hearth** <term>focum</term> <note>original: "focum"; Latin for fireplace or focus-point of the heat.</note> and at the top a good deal wider than at the bottom. Afterward, fill it with fine lining, one third from the top and one part from the side, and make it nice and smooth. And a **cupel** <term>Cüpell</term> will be filled halfway in the furnace; plug it very small. And make there a **hearth-bed** <term>Berst</term> for the furnace and melt, when the instructions have been correctly written for me.

### On the Removal of Iron Slag and 
### their Character.
<note>The "iron thorn" (Eisen dorn) refers to the metallic spikes or slag that form during the smelting process.</note>

Take iron and soften it well with the essence of Gold <term>$\unicode{x2609}$</term> <note>original: Sol/Gold; the sun symbol represents gold in alchemy.</note> and break it in two; then, so that you do not simply lose the metal, make a hearth-pipe and keep the fire there for three or four hours long, so that the pipe subjects the lead.

### The Silver Can Be Used 
### in This Manner.

For this, take one Mark <note>A traditional unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 230 grams.</note> of pure silver and place it in a **crucible** <term>Tiegel</term>, which must be constantly agitated or "saturated" <note>original: "truncken"; literally 'drunk,' implying the metal has absorbed as much of an additive as possible.</note> until it turns black.

### How Gold is Made from Copper, 
### or how they should be separated 
### or divided.
<note>The original heading uses "Solem A Venere," referring to the alchemical symbols for Gold (Sol) and Copper (Venus).</note>

Take the "body" <note>The physical metallic mass.</note> in which the Gold and Copper are now joined together and sink it into a crucible! Then take **Sulfur** <term>Sulphur</term> and iron scales or **Hematite** <term>Eisen glantz</term> in equal parts <term>p. p.</term> <note>original: "partes pro"; proportional parts.</note>.

<margin>
The instructions for when one should perform these tasks so that they succeed or endure are shown and taught above.
</margin>

### If You Wish to Refine the Silver 
### or Perform Calcination.
<note>original: "Verbrennung"; literally 'burning,' but in this context, it refers to calcination, the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile impurities.</note>

Then add one part per Mark of Gold <term>$\unicode{x2609}$</term> and Copper <term>$\unicode{x2640}$</term> and an equal weight of the additive, and it requires <meta>catchword: namely</meta>

<column-break/>

namely, the prepared silver, to which a quarter-measure of **Litharge** <term>lithargyrum</term> <note>A secondary mineral form of lead oxide, often called "silver dross" or "silver glance" (Silber gleit) in old texts.</note> is added; let it flow together in the crucible. If the silver is significantly covered, then so much litharge should be added that it is completely submerged. Even if you then calcine it in the crucible many times, it will never return to its initial state.

### Another Useful Separation 
### of Gold and Copper.

Take one part pure Copper <term>$\unicode{x2640}$</term> and equal parts of available copper—the kind of copper shells made from burnt bones—and heat it in a pan. Add salt brine and a little **Mercury** <term>$\unicode{x260c}$</term>. Let it cook and boil so that the corrosive ash does its work. If it will not separate or combine, add more salt and it will separate. But if you do not wish to separate it, you must not add the Sulfur. Afterward, take copper sheets and common salt and layer them **layer upon layer** <term>s/s/s</term> <note>original: "stratum super stratum"; a common alchemical method of layering materials to ensure even reaction.</note>. Then make a fire beneath it so that your sheets completely calcine the copper. Then take that same copper and throw in a portion of quickly warmed copper-scales; the gold will fall to the bottom. Take of the same in equal parts **Saltpeter** <term>Salis Nitrij</term> and one part Sulfur.

### The Talent <term>Talentum</term>
Is a weight, called so by everyone (it is called a "pound" in Holy Scripture). However, it is of three kinds: the large talent, the small, and the medium talent. The small talent contains 40 pounds <term>libras</term>, the medium contains 70 pounds, but the highest and largest talent contains 120 pounds. Thus writes and says Isidore <note>referring to Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose encyclopedic works were a standard reference for medieval and early modern science.</note>.

->Now follows further, and here begins an Alchemical book whose title is contained in the following verses etc.<-

> After **SIM**, **SUM** follows, and the final **MOON** <note>original: *LUNA*</note> is placed below.
> I calcine, I sublime / I bear, I fix, I coagulate, I dissolve:
> From these, the stone is thus made, which brings many joys.
<note>The words "SIM" and "SUM" are mnemonics for the planets: Saturn, Jupiter (Iuppiter), Mars / Sol (Sun), Venus (written as Uenus), and Mercury.</note>

This verse indicates the order of the planets as they stand one after another in the heavens.

<margin>$\unicode{x2644}$ Saturn / Lead</margin>
The first and highest planet is Saturn; it is noted by the letter S. It completes its course through the 12 heavenly signs in 30 years, 5 days, and 6 hours.

<margin>$\unicode{x2643}$ Jupiter / Tin</margin>
The second planet is Jupiter; it is noted by the letter J. It completes its course through the Zodiac once in 12 years.

<margin>$\unicode{x2642}$ Mars / Iron</margin>
After this follows MARS; it is indicated by the word M. It runs through the Zodiac once every 7 years. <note>The author provides 7 years here, though the astronomical period of Mars is roughly 2 years.</note>

<margin>$\unicode{x2609}$ Sun / Gold</margin>

The second and third works indicate the **Principles**, with which the artist labors and deals in his Mastery <term>Magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process</term>, and from these, he brings together his works or whatever he wishes to create. There are, however, five principles mentioned of these things: **Calcination** <term>burning to ash</term>, **Sublimation** <term>vaporizing and solidifying</term>, **Grinding** <note>original: *Contritio*</note> or rubbing down, **Coagulation** <term>thickening a liquid to a solid</term>, and finally **Solution** <term>dissolving</term>. At the beginning of this book, each of these principles is explained more specifically: namely **sublimation**, **descending** <note>original: *Descensio*; a process of distillation by heat from above</note>, **distillation**, **calcination**, **solution**, **coagulation**, **fixation** <term>making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>, and **softening** <note>original: *Ceratio*; the process of making a substance wax-like or soft</note>. ### Also for Copper Embossing /

Take a piece of leather that has been purged and cleaned on the inside, and is unspun, or lay herring-water <note>likely a brine or pickling liquid from preserved fish</note> upon it in thin layers, a finger thick. ### For *Aurum Musicum* <note>original: *Auro Musico*; also known as "Mosaic Gold," a tin-based pigment used to imitate gold in manuscripts</note>, the rich gold with which one writes /

Take **the Sun** <note>original: *Solem*; the alchemical name for Gold</note> which has been beaten very fine or ground. And grind it well in a smooth tray with **liquid honey** <note>original: *Honigseim*; the finest, purest honey that flows naturally from the comb</note> until it becomes a pulp. After this, take a **receptacle** <note>original: *Lochman*; likely a crucible or specific pot</note> of the **furnace** <note>original: *Cheminy*; literally "chimney," referring here to the heating chamber</note> and fill it half full with pure water. To this, place it upon the fire until it begins to melt and flow together, and then set it aside again. Beforehand, pour well-dissolved **Gold** <note>original: *Solem*</note> into a water that was previously poured out, and then set aside the substance or material that shimmers white on top. Pour it in, and so you shall find **Gold** <note>original: *Solem*</note> which, when tempered or mixed with egg white, you can use to write so that it flows very well from the pen and glistens.

### Also another way to make such Mosaic Gold

Take a hen’s egg from the brood <gloss>original: *Omen Ovum pullorum*; "an egg from a brood of chicks"</gloss> and pour out everything that is in the egg. After this, take some of it and lay this substance in a baking oven after the water has been removed, and augment it well, and give it fire thereafter.

### To make Azure <note>original: *Lazurium*; a blue pigment</note>

This may refer to a straining material or a specific botanical resin.</note>, and a little **honey** or **mead** <note>original: *Weinmi*, likely *Weinmet*.</note> or **olive oil** <note>original: *Safft von Baumoy*, literally "juice of tree-oil."</note>. Likewise, if you wish to bring about **dregs** <term>faces</term><note>Latin: *faeces*, meaning sediment or dregs.</note>, take sharp **vinegar** and pour it onto the dregs, and the liquid which is poured off from the food <note>This likely refers to the liquid separated from the pigment mass.</note>. And then pour it out two or three times. But as for those [pigments] given, **compose** or mix them as has been prescribed.

# Of the Gold which is written with a pen

Take **Sun Gold** <gloss>Solen</gloss><note>The alchemical term for pure gold.</note> burned by fire, and grind it very well upon a stone. And sprinkle it with **salt**—red salt—upon each **plate** <gloss>Tabulae</gloss>, and afterward rub it very strongly upon a stone. And let the **paste** <note>original: *Pflaster*.</note> boil out cleanly, and the **calcined powder** <term>Calcinn</term> beforehand with **water**. And wash it clean and often, until the salt has completely left it and the substance of the gold remains there. And then temper it with **Gum Arabic**, and write with it using a **pen**. And **burnish** the writing, or one glazes it a little with a **horse tooth**. Likewise, there is another way of using **burnt gold** for painting: if it is [to be] laid, one can also write it with a pen. For this, **Mercury** <term>Mercurius</term><note>Quicksilver.</note> is first extraordinarily applied upon a **marble stone**, and then ground upon a stone, and **tempered** with Gum Arabic, and finally made **burnished** or shiny with a horse tooth. And it is to be known that the painted mixtures or **temperas** can be written upon any thing.

### How you wish to make <term>Viride Rodagum</term> <note>A copper-based green pigment, often a variant of verdigris.</note>
Take very pure copper plates and coat them thoroughly on both sides with the best <term>soap</term> <note>original: *Scheiffen*</note> from the saltworks; then put them into a new pot and fill it with very sharp or strong wine. Seal it well and cover it with pitch, and set it for nine or 15 days in a warm place. Afterwards, open the pot and shake or scrape off that which is on the plates onto a wooden tablet, and dry it in the sun.

### How you wish to make <term>Viride Grum</term> or Greek green
Take a large new pot and put very pure copper plates into it <gloss>And you should hang the plates from a cord of Cyprus [copper] or steel</gloss> <note>The Latin gloss specifies using wire to suspend the metal, ensuring maximum exposure to the vapors.</note> and set the plates straight. Fill the pot with very sour vinegar or with <term>ripe wine</term> <note>original: *gewinn* or *zeitigen wein*</note>, and then seal the pot and set it in a warm place for up to 6 months. Afterwards, open the pot and whatever you find therein, take it and lay it upon a wooden tablet and dry it in the sun.

### How you wish to make red <term>Minium</term> or red lead
Take a new clay pot and put plates of lead into it. Fill the pot with very sharp vinegar and seal it up, and set it in <term>manure</term> <note>Dung was frequently used in alchemy and pigment-making as a source of steady, gentle heat and carbon dioxide.</note> in a warm place. Afterwards, open it, and whatever has attached itself to the plates in the pot, shake or scrape it off into another clay vessel. Put it all into the fire and stir it constantly or continually until it has become red like <term>Minium</term> or red lead <note>original: *Menning*</note>. Then remove it from the fire and let it become cold in the vessel.

### How you wish to make <term>Vermiculum</term> or cinnabar
Take a glass flask and one weight of **quicksilver** <note>original: *Argenti Viui*; mercury.</note> and two weights of white sulfur or <term>saffron</term> <note>While the text says *Saffran*, cinnabar is typically made from mercury and sulfur; the author may be referring to the color or a specific additive.</note>. Place or put them into a flask and set it by the fire, and shake it constantly over a gentle glowing fire. Cover the flask from above with another and smaller flask, and when you find a smoke arising like **Vermiculum** or **cinnabar** <note>original: *Zinober*</note>, then take the flask away; it should have what you desire.

### Also, how you wish to make green colors,
### with which you [can] **illuminate books**
### [of] the **delightful art** <note>A common historical term for the art of painting and decoration.</note>.

Take **copper sheets** and <unclear>coat</unclear> them with **honey**; after that, take **salt**, burn it in the fire, and pulverize it over [the sheets]. After this, fill a box halfway with strong wine; then hang the copper sheets in the box, but in such a way that they do not touch the wine. Place a lid on the box and seal it very well, and let it stand in **manure** <note>original: *Mist*; decaying manure was used as a consistent, gentle heat source for chemical reactions.</note>. Every eight days the manure should be renewed; and let it stand for a day or eight, or for some time, and you will obtain a very good color.

# If you want to make good Ink
Take egg yolks separated from the whites and burn them in a small, narrow pot; afterwards, distemper it <note>To "distemper" means to mix the pigment with a binder (like glue or egg) to make paint.</note>, and a good **ink** <note>original: *Incaustrum*; here referring to a dark pigment or ink made from charred organic matter.</note> will be produced.

# A silver color
Take beaten silver in sheets or plates, add **mercury** <note>original: *Argentum Vivum*</note> to it, and set it on the fire until the vapor from the **mercury** escapes. # How one shall shape Quicksilver, along with how to make it white through Sublimation.

Take Quicksilver <term>Argentum Vivum: liquid mercury</term> which is good and purified or cleansed of lead and all other filth. Mix it with good vitriol <note>original: "de Calchanto bono"; vitriol refers to sulfate minerals used for their acidic and reactive properties</note>, and take instead of vinegar <note>original: "Stat der Einig"; likely a misspelling of "Essig" (vinegar), which appears later in the recipe</note> and persist with the fixation until all the Quicksilver is coagulated <note>thickened or solidified</note> and nothing more of it is found in the vitriol. Afterward, dry it and take it away from the moisture so that it is stiff, and lay it between two pans <term>Patellen: shallow earthenware or metal dishes used as a simple distillation apparatus</term>. Seal them <term>Verlutire: to seal a vessel airtight using "lute," a paste of clay, lime, or dung</term> with clay or loam, and set them upon the fire. Maintain a fire beneath them for about as long as it takes for meat to be cooked. Afterward, take the pans away from the fire and let them cool; then take them and open them. You will find that one part of the Quicksilver has attached itself to the upper pan, and that part is "dead," while the other is "living" <note>the "dead" part is the chemically transformed white sublimate, while the "living" part remains liquid metal</note>. Collect or gather all of it together, and if a piece remains nearby, apply it and press or drip vinegar <note>original: "Essig oder Essit"</note> upon it. Lay it again between the two pans and seal the edges or lips with clay, and set it over the fire as you did before. Do all this seven times, or a little more or less, until it becomes white; thereby you serve and keep it.

## Egg oil is made thus

Take as many hard egg yolks as you wish, and crush them well in a mortar, and put them into a glass vessel. Seal the vessel well at the top so that it does not leak <note>original: "ausrauche"; literally "smoke out" or evaporate</note>. Place it under horse manure <note>a common alchemical method for providing a steady, gentle heat for fermentation or digestion</note> for three whole weeks. Afterward, take the glass out and distill it through an alembic <term>an alchemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>; thus you have an oil that descends as a yellow liquid. This same oil can also be made over a long time with egg whites, but you must distill it with a gentle and clear fire.

# A practice of Master Jacob of
## Viterbo to be applied to Tinwork

Place or set **Tin** <note>original: "♃" or "Jupiter," the alchemical symbol for tin</note> into a conical **tin-stone** <note>original: "Zapfen Zinnstein"; likely a cone-shaped piece of cassiterite or tin ore</note>, and once the tin is dissolved, pour it out into a dry crucible, and pour a good **plaster of Orpiment** <note>original: "pflaster Aur"; likely *Auripigmentum* (arsenic trisulfide), used to give metals a golden color</note> over it; then set another perforated crucible inverted upon it, so that a pipe can pass through it. There, take the **Tin** <note>original: "♃"</note> from the fire, dissolve it, and afterwards pour it through a pipe into vinegar three or four times, until it becomes purified and clear. After that, take an equal amount of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij ☿"</note> and pour it into the molten tin, and stir it constantly in the crucible until it becomes gray. Then, polish it until it takes on a silver color, and have a **lithostone glass** <note>original: "lüftsteinnes glas"; likely a heat-resistant vessel made of or containing refined minerals</note> with a narrow and long neck and a **sealed mouth** <note>original: "lütum os"; a mouth closed with alchemical lute/sealing clay</note>. Afterwards, take **Sal Ammoniac** <note>original: "Salarmoniacum"; ammonium chloride</note> and **sulfur** in the same weight as the **Tin** <note>original: "♃"</note> is; grind them together and place them with the others in a glass. Set the glass in an **ash-pit** <note>original: "aschen fall"; a sand or ash bath for even heating</note> up to the neck, but the vessel or pot should be full of ashes. Seal it and always light a fire beneath it, and support the glass with a small **piston** <note>original: "Bisten"; perhaps a rod or support</note>. And
<meta>catchword: let it come</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>292</page-num>

let it come day and night. And then, [when it is] cold, break the glass; there you will find the clear substance below and **Cinnabar** <note>original: "Zinobier"; mercury sulfide</note> above, which is the thing required for this art, as is the other common cinnabar, for **Gold** <note>original: "☉" or "Sol"</note>. God be praised and thanked.

---

## A Water of Saturn or Lead Water
### which empowers all bodies

Take lead filings or **blind ore** <note>original: "Steiner blinde"; likely galena or a dull lead mineral</note>, one pound, and [add] as much plaster as there is tin. Place an equal amount of lead therewith, and let it stand until it is all dissolved. Stir it several times every day, and a black matter will remain in the other part of the housing; from this, strain the water from the **dregs** <note>original: "feirig fari gewand oder umschach"; archaic terms for residue or the process of separation</note>, and throw the black matter away. With this water, all **bodies** <note>original: "Corper"; metals</note> and stones are dissolved in a most wonderful manner. Therefore, with this water, you shall attain that which you desire to achieve. Thanks be to God.

---

# Note on the General Christian Faith

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ says: Not all who say to me, "Lord, Lord," and so forth <note>Matthew 7:21</note>. And the Apostle says: There is one God, one faith, one baptism <note>Ephesians 4:5</note>. Likewise: They all indeed run, but only one comes first <note>1 Corinthians 9:24</note>. Likewise Saint Augustine in *On the Faith, to Peter*, clearly shows in the last chapter concerning the *Hereticis* or heretics, very strongly: You must not doubt at all, for it is false that those among heretics or schismatics do not participate and have fellowship with the Devil and his angels in his compendium. If such a person before his end has not been incorporated <note>original: "incorporirt oder niederleibtet"; literally "embodied into"</note> into the holy Christian church. So says he <note>original: "Hæc ille"</note>.

<margin>And never in the</margin>

# Of Saltpeter

Take salt in a basin <note>original: "Paschen"; a small vessel or pan</note>, as much as you want, and add to it an equal amount of wine. However much you put the salt in, and when it is well-formed, the salt is incorporated or embodied. Thereafter, place it in a basin on the fire and let it boil until it becomes water <note>liquefies</note> together, and stir it through and through constantly and well. Once more let it boil until, from that salt, "Royal Water" <note>original: "Aqua Regis"; a highly corrosive mixture of acids, though here used as a stage in the recipe</note> is made, until a stone forms from the salt on top. Thereafter, pour the same stone onto the salt, while it—just as in the sun—never settles into hardness. And thus you will have and obtain good saltpeter <note>original: "Salnitri"</note>.

# Of Red Mars ♂

Take "green of copper" <note>original: "Viride æris"; verdigris or copper acetate</note> or green copper-stone as much as you want; lay it in a basin with the heat. Place the **iron** <note>original: "Martem"; Mars is the alchemical symbol for iron</note> inside it, and let it boil well with the heat for a day. And once it has surged up, let it dry, and thereafter let it boil again. Afterward take vitriol <note>a metal sulfate, often used as a corrosive or for coloring</note>, grind it to powder, place it in the basin, and on top of it place iron filings <note>original: "Limaturam Martis"</note>. And continue to fill it, and increase or make the fire always larger and stronger. Let it stand in the fire for four or five hours, and thus you will have made it well.

## A water which makes all metals soft
Take burnt brick, Edres salt <note>possibly a regional term for a specific mineral salt or common salt</note>, tartar, and <term>Sal Armoniacum</term> <note>original: "Sal Armoniacum"; Sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride), used as a powerful flux in metallurgy</note> <term>Ana</term> <note>original: "Ana"; a term meaning 'equal parts of each'</note>. Pulverize them very finely and add an oil to them as described hereafter; boil the metal in vinegar with these ingredients. Then soak the metal and let it boil once more in the mentioned <term>Aceto</term> <note>Latin: "Aceto"; vinegar or acetic acid</note> or vinegar. Afterwards, wash it again. Do this three times, or as long as it takes until the metal becomes pliable or soft.

---

## To transform silver into gold
Take burnt copper, <term>Sal Armoniacum</term>, crushed <term>Vitrioll</term> <note>original: "Vitrioll"; metal sulfates, typically iron or copper sulfate, used for their corrosive and reactive properties</note>, and <term>Crocum Martis</term> <note>Latin: "Crocum Martis"; 'Saffron of Mars,' a reddish iron oxide powder</note> <term>Ana</term>. Pulverize and mix them together with tree oil <note>usually olive oil</note>. Throw this mixture onto molten silver—it should be one-third part like gold—and let them boil together in a goldsmith’s crucible for one hour.

---

## A cementation of gold
Take gold and place it in a crucible. To every mark <note>a traditional weight for precious metals, roughly 230 grams</note> of gold, add 18 grains of cemented copper. When it melts, add one <term>Quintlein</term> <note>a small unit of weight, about 3.75 grams</note> of <term>Salis</term> <note>Latin: "Salis"; salt</note> and pour it out of the crucible. Clean the crucible thoroughly once more and melt the mixture three times.

<column-break/>

<page-num>296.</page-num>

## A water for jewels
Take as much burnt copper as you wish and make it glowing hot. Place it back into tree oil and let the oil dry into it thoroughly. Boil away half of the oil, then take more oil and repeat the process with the burnt copper ten times. Afterward, take as much of this prepared copper as you wish and melt it together with fine, pure <term>Luna</term> <note>Latin: "Luna"; the alchemical name for silver</note>. Then take as much warm <term>Sole</term> <note>Latin: "Sole" (Sol); the alchemical name for gold</note> as there is silver and copper mixed together. Melt them all together, and whatever you produce from this material, it will have "degrees" <note>indicating a high level of purity, quality, or "rank" in the alchemical hierarchy</note>.

---

## **Of Sal Ammoniac**

I wish to teach and instruct you how you should make and prepare a **Sal Ammoniac** <term>Sal Armoniack</term> <note>ammonium chloride; a vital salt in alchemy used to dissolve metals and act as a flux</note>, which you might not be able to obtain in your land because of the distance and the great forests. Place into it as much of the **soot** <term>Ruß</term> as hangs in the baskets <note>likely referring to the collection baskets or flues in a chimney</note>, which is made from and grown out of smoke. Take 10 pounds of this. Rub it down and place it inside, and let it boil three times. But watch this carefully when it boils or surges up, so that it does not run out of the cauldron. However, you must let it boil until the saturation <note>the liquid</note> has consumed half the salt and it is taken in. Then put pure water in it, to full measure, and let the dregs settle. Pour off the clearer and purer liquid, and **boil it down** <note>original: *decoquire*; to reduce a liquid by boiling</note> again until the **moisture** <term>Humiditates</term> <note>original: *Humiditates*; liquids or humidity</note> has evaporated and it becomes thick. Now, when it has begun to thicken together, take that which has become thick out with a spoon and place it in a strong pot until everything is prepared and obtained; otherwise, the cauldron would be destroyed and shattered. This would be my advice: that you lay a linen cloth over it so that it may be dried by the sun, or in the oven after the bread has been taken out. Sublimate this salt three times.

### If You Wish to Make Cinnabar

Take 2 parts <term>Argentum Vivum</term> <note>Latin: "living silver" or quicksilver/mercury</note> and 1 part <term>Sulfur</term> <note>originally abbreviated *sul.*</note>, or clean sulfur. Make

a gentle fire, until the water [gives off] the <term>Vapores</term> <note>vapors</note> or exhalations, which you should test in this manner: place a knife upon it. And when the glow no longer strikes out, then the Cinnabar is pure and perfectly made.

### A Purification of Mercury

->Note<-

The <term>Argentum Vivum</term> is purified thus: First, grind it in a wooden or stone mortar with vinegar and common salt until the salt becomes black. Afterward, separate the Mercury from the salt with warm water, and do this frequently <term>according to custom</term> <note>original: *secundum Gebrauch*; following standard alchemical practice</note>.

How one should purify Mercury in other ways, you may see in the Catalog, as you may have been informed previously.

# How One Should Indurate or Make Mercury Hard

Take a metallic vessel and place the Mercury inside; pour tree oil <note>original: *Baum-ölln*; historically referring to olive oil or a similar vegetable oil</note> over it, and set it upon a gentle fire. Watch closely to ensure that the smoke does not escape. Let it melt or repeat the process five or seven times, and for the last time, pour good <term>acetate</term> <note>original: *Atzet*; strong vinegar or acetic acid</note> or vinegar into it. Let it simmer in the vinegar until it is thoroughly <unclear>absorbed</unclear>; then, the Mercury will become hard, such that one can work it with a hammer upon the anvil.

# Saint Thomas Aquinas
<note>Thomas Aquinas was frequently cited in alchemical manuscripts, though most works attributed to him are considered pseudo-epigraphical (written by others in his name).</note>

Take 1 ounce of Silver and 1 part <term>Braminis</term> <note>an obscure term, likely referring to a specific lead-based ore or mineral</note> of the ore, as much Lead as the previous two, and as much Sulfur as these three all together. Thereafter, melt the Silver and the <term>Bramen</term> together, and then mix the Lead into it. After this, add a little at a time of <term>Silphir</term> <note>a variant spelling of *Sulfur*</note> or Sulfur, and let them all burn away at the same time. Finally, let it brighten or <term>gleam</term> <note>original: *blicken*; a technical term for the moment a precious metal becomes pure in a cupel</note>; thus you will obtain the best Silver, which is tenacious and suitable for coinage, and which remains steadfast and proven in all tests or fires. The writer of these numbers <note>likely referring to the proportions</note> is this Doctor, Thomas Aquinas.

### A Calcination of Lead by Archelaus
<note>Archelaus was a 5th-century BCE Greek philosopher, often cited in alchemy as a teacher of Socrates and a master of the "stone."</note>

Take Lead <term>Saturn</term> <note>original: *saturni*; the planetary name for lead</note>, as much as you wish, melt it, and quench it three times in common hard salt water. This salt should be prepared and dissolved in very sharp vinegar mixed with 2 lbs of honey. Afterward, grind it up and place it for three days and nights in an oven. In the morning, draw it out again, and you will find a white and powerful <term>calx</term> <note>the fine powder or oxide left after a metal has been roasted or chemically treated</note>, the most beautiful of all. You may calcine Tin <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: *Jovem*; the planetary name for tin</note> in the same manner, only you must quench it more often—namely, nine times.

### A Righteous, True, and Philosophical Calcination of All Bodies

Take Mercury, sublimate it, and afterward imbue it with fixed <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note> water—that is, with oil of tartar and the lime of bird eggshells. Sublimate it again, and take that which rises to the top. Place 1 lb of this upon 10 lbs of any molten metal, and it will be calcined with a complete calcination. This is proven and true.

### To Make Gold: A Practical, True, and Well-Proven Experiment with Oil of Iron Added, which is Self-Made

<meta>catchword: Place iron</meta>

<column-break/>

Place iron in a pot and fill it full. The pot should have <term>foramina</term> <note>original: *foramina*; holes or openings</note> or holes through the bottom. Seal the top with stones or the lid. Make a fire beneath or over the pot so that the oil descends—that is, appears below—and falls through the holes into a vessel placed underneath with a gentle fire. With this oil, <term>incerate</term> <note>from the Latin *incerare*; to mix a dry substance with liquid or oil until it reaches a waxy consistency</note> the sublimated mercury seven times—or the arsenic—upon a marble stone, and rub it well with the aforementioned oil. Afterward, distill it in warm sand and then coagulate it in a glass ampoule in a warm baker’s oven, which should be placed in a soft wool bath. One part of this coagulated Mercury, when added to 30 lbs of Silver <term>Luna</term> <note>original: *lunæ*; the planetary name for silver</note>, transforms it into Gold <term>Sol</term> <note>original: *solem*; the planetary name for gold</note>. And note that this is no different than the <term>fictitious</term> <note>original: *fingierte* or *fictis*; here meaning an alchemically created or "philosophical" metal rather than a mined one</note> ones; therefore, draw the oil from the iron extract and proceed.

### It Produces Gold

<margin>
The medicine
</margin>
Take Lead <note>original: *saturnum*</note>, copper, brass, cinnabar, <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: *Auripigmentum*; a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, sal ammoniac, and alum. Tint them and place them in a glazed pot. ### A Downward Distillation through a Bearded Pot
### or Filter
<note>original: *Botum barbatum*; a specific alchemical crucible with a perforated bottom used for downward distillation.</note>

### A Purification of Copper into Silver

Take 1 part of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: *Salis Armoniaci*; ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note> and 2 parts of good, pure glass. Rub them together and turn them into powder. After that, take 7 parts of copper sheet and melt them into small pieces and parts. When you have melted the copper, divide the aforementioned powder into nine parts and throw 1 part of the ground powder upon the copper that has been dissolved by the fire. Let them boil thoroughly together. When it is added, pour good <term>honey</term> <note>original: *rauch honig*; raw or "smoke" honey</note> upon it. Proceed in the same manner and use the remaining parts of the powder and the copper, and you will have <term>Silver</term> <note>original: *Lunam*</note> afterward.

<meta>This page continues the alchemical instructions for the transmutation of metals, specifically moving from the planetary correspondences of the previous page to practical recipes for gold-making, the preparation of alkali salts, red lead (minium), and a recipe for gold ink. ### To Transform Silver into Gold

Take burnt copper <note>calcined copper</note>, sal ammoniac, mercury, vitriol, salt of the sea <note>original: "Corum Maris", likely a corruption of "Sal Maris"</note> etc. Pulverize these and temper or mix them with skill. A tincture <note>original: "Zucht", referring here to a concentrated extract or "seed" of the metal</note> is then drawn out, one-sixteenth part, of which the other three parts should be stone or pure wax. Let them flow and melt together in a goldsmith’s crucible for one hour.

### A Distillation of Alkali Salt

When you reach the point where the water is all present, let it remain in the lining <note>possibly the vessel lining or a specific container</note>, and keep it until the morning. Then let it settle in a boiler <note>original: "Caldario", a hot-water vessel</note> until all the water disappears. However, the water should not steam or give off an unpleasant smoke. Then let it cool, and it will become a hard stone, which is called **Alkali Salt** <term>Sal Alkali: a basic salt, typically potassium carbonate or sodium carbonate, essential in alchemical fluxing</term>, which is the **Dregs of Bitterness** <note>original: "Fax Amaritudinis"</note>. Take the third part and place it in a jar until it is half full, and set the jar in an open furnace or a blast-furnace <note>original: "Buerreschloß-sammen Offen", likely a furnace with a specific draft-locking mechanism</note>. Give it a very gentle fire so that it is not ruined or burnt away when it settles. Afterward, give it a better or stronger fire until it becomes entirely red and glows like a flash <note>original: "blicke", referring to the "blick" or sudden brightening of molten silver when impurities are removed</note>. It will soften just like wax; then draw it out. Strike the iron against the jar to loosen it into another jar as quickly as you can, so that you do not delay with the extraction. If you linger, some material will remain in the jar in such a way that you can no longer pour it out, and thus you would must obtain new Alkali Salt. Place this in a glass vessel in a warm place; let it become dry and guard it well. If you place it in a damp place, it will be dissolved into water.

---

...it is made like red lead or minium <term>Minium: a bright red-orange lead oxide used as a pigment and in alchemy</term>, and let it cool in the same vessel. Thus you will find red lead or minium.

### If You Want to Make the Best Red Lead

Take a large glass sphere and smear the outside with loam or clay so that it remains intact and does not crack or shatter even in a great heat of the embers. Set it upon three or four stones or crucibles, and place into it two parts of sulfur, saffron-colored yellow cedarwood <note>original: "Crocci gelbes Zedrenholz"; "Crocus" usually refers to a saffron-colored metallic oxide</note>, and a weight of antimony <note>original: "Antarit", likely a variant of "Antimonium"</note>. Then make a gentle fire with three scoops <note>original: "kellen", likely referring to measures of fuel or bellows-strokes</note> and cover the jar. And when you see a red smoke coming out, take the jar off the fire. Whatever you find inside, keep it or save it.

### If You Want to Make a Golden Script

Take alum and let it melt. When it has melted, take gold and wash it or work it for a long time with this liquid <note>original: "liquore"</note> or water in a brewer’s vat or in a mortar. When it is whole, rub it again upon a stone with gum arabic. Temper it in the fatherly way <note>possibly a specific traditional method</note> with pumice stone <note>original: "Keibestein"</note>. # If you wish to <gloss>cast</gloss> a crystal as you please
Warm it in a crucible <note>original: "crucibulo", a ceramic or graphite melting pot</note> or a melting pan, and burn it thoroughly. Afterward, throw it into water to quench it. After this, grind it into a powder that is fine, small, and subtle. Add to this powder a fourth part of alkali salt <term>Salis Alkali: a basic salt used as a flux to lower the melting point of minerals</term> and saltpeter <term>Salis Nitri: potassium nitrate, used here to aid the melting process</term>. Then combine them to form a "body" <note>a unified mass</note>, place it into the hottest glassmaker's furnace <note>original: "fornacem Vitreatorum calidissimam"</note>, and set it in a very warm blast furnace. Whatever quality it possesses afterward, you may cast it into molds as you desire. Without these two salts, it cannot be melted at all, *because just as its existence [comes about] by means of excessive cold, so too its dissolution occurs in the same way, which does not fail* <note>original Latin: "quia sicut in esse per modum nimiae frigiditatis, ita fit eiusdem resolutio quae non fallit." This reflects the ancient belief that rock crystal was water frozen so intensely that it became permanent stone.</note>. That is to say: just as its being was formed from excessive and great cold, so also is its dissolution, and not otherwise.

# If you wish to have the crystal green or red
If you wish to make this, once it has been melted in the manner and way described, add to it powder of ultramarine lazuli <note>original: "pulverem Lazurij transmarini", a blue pigment made from lapis lazuli, though the text suggests it can create other colors</note>, and it will take on a color. If the powder is green, the crystal will also become green. Such a crystal, however, cannot be distinguished from common ones that are good or precious, as it also follows its own properties and nature; therefore, it cannot be identified as different even by the variation of colors.

# How one should cast or melt the crystal
Take borax stone <note>original: "Borassthein"</note>, as soon as it has been opened, and larch blossoms when they are in bloom; knead these in place of the crystal described below. Place that same crystal in warm ashes, and whatever it contains, lay it upon warm silk. Afterward, take one part of prepared lead and two parts of crystal; to both of these, take powdered marble. Put them together into the crystal, and cast or melt it as you like.

# How one should make crystal or other stones soft
Take the urine of a billy-goat and the blood of a billy-goat; mix them together. Afterward, take the crystal or other stones, whichever you wish, and lay them on hot silk. Maintain this for several days so that you are always adding or laying warm things to it, as they are kept in such a confection or mixture. Then the crystal or the stone will become so soft that it can be cut; this is a true and good work for making crystal and other stones soft.

## To make glass-gall clarifier or to make glass white,

Take dark lead <note>likely antimony or bismuth, used to decolorize glass</note> and water-lead <note>likely graphite or molybdenite</note> and treat them in a little copper-water <note>original: "Küpfferwasser", a solution of copper vitriol or sulfate</note> colored with it; however, take fine linden-wood "thorns" <note>likely fine shavings or charcoal from the lime tree</note>. ### If you wish to make atrament or black ink

## To make gemstones soft

Take captured spring water, put it in a glass pot, lay the stones inside, and let them stand therein for 12 days.

## For boils or frostbite on the hands

Take ivy resin <note>original: "Gummi Hedera"</note>—as much as you wish—and distill it with a little oil; then rub or salve the hands with it. On that same day, one will feel no boils or frostbite. To this, you may also take distilled nettles <note>original: "Nesselz"</note> and dip them therein.

## How one shall make gold and silver filings, which are commonly used for mining purposes and especially for heart or stomach medicine.

Take a piece of good and pure gold and have before you a basin <note>original: "Parastidem"; a shallow vessel or support</note> or mirror-vessel with wooden-water <note>possibly water held in a wooden container or treated with wood-ash</note>, and also have a clean, rough, or coarse linen cloth. Hold one end in your hand; the other should be stretched out and fastened to the bottom of the basin or bowl in the water. Then rub or grate the gold upon the cloth, making sure that you always keep the cloth wet or moist with water. In this way, the filings <note>original: "limatura"</note> or the gold dust fall down to the bottom of the bowl. Continue doing this until enough has been formed from the gold, as much as you wish to have. Let the filings lie therein for one hour, and draw the water off very gently and with caution; wash the filings three times, make them dry, and keep them. Do exactly the same with silver <note>original: "Argento"</note>. There are some who find that the gold should be filed very subtly and small, and then used for the same purpose.

## How one shall make Cinifur, that is, Cinnabar.

Take quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti Vivi"</note> and yellow sulfur <note>original: "Sulphuris"</note> in equal parts <note>original: "ana"</note> (though some take less sulfur than quicksilver). Mix them together and place it all in a glazed earthenware vessel which

<column-break/>

can withstand the fire. Fill the third part of the vessel with the medicine or mixture; let the other two parts remain empty. Afterward, close the vessel with a glazed lid or clay, and seal them together <term>Lute: to seal a vessel with "lute," a paste made of clay, dung, or lead to make it airtight</term> well with loam and mortar or another mixture. Following this, build a square oven and set the vessel in the middle of the square oven, so that the two parts of the vessel which were left empty above the medicine reach out above the square oven. The bottom of the vessel should stand as high from the floor or hearth of the oven as the width of two hands. Then light a fire underneath it and maintain the same for a full 12 hours. After this, let the oven become cold, then break the vessel, and you will find Cinnabar <note>original: "Zinnifer oder Zinnober"; a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide</note>.

## Making a Sal Ammoniac <note>original: "Sal Armoniack"; ammonium chloride, a volatile salt highly valued in alchemy for its ability to dissolve metals</note>
Take as much of the **Sal Ammoniac** as you wish, and grind it well, and pour upon it good **wine** or **spirit of wine** <note>high-proof brandy or ethanol</note> which is not sour, but sweet, so that the **Sal Ammoniac** is dissolved therein. And that which becomes dissolved, keep and preserve it in a glass **ampulla** <note>a small, round vial</note>. The remainder of the **Sal Ammoniac**, make it dry. And in whichever <term>formulas</term> <note>original: "kützten"; likely a variant of "Skizzen" or "Künsten," meaning recipes or arts</note> the **Sal Ammoniac** is renewed, so that it shall be used and employed as a medicine, then keep for yourself this **Sal Ammoniac** which has been thus prepared.

## To make Azure from Magnesia
Take **Magnesia**, which is called **smelt** <note>original: "Schmelts"; likely referring to manganese dioxide, used as a flux or decoloring agent in glassmaking</note>, and which is fine, pure, and bright or light. Grind it to a powder; therefore, <term>imbibe</term> <note>soak or saturate</note> the same powder with **Sal Ammoniac water** three, four, or five times, and let it also dry often each time. But when you have imbibed it for the last time, do not let it dry out, but lay it all while still moist or wet upon a linen cloth, and place it over the hot steam in another vessel, arranged in the manner of **Nedo’s Fire** <note>original: "Fuers Nedonis"; likely a reference to a specific alchemical vapor bath or gentle heat method</note>. And stop up that same vessel well at the top

<meta>catchword: damitt</meta>

<column-break/>

so that nothing can **evaporate** <note>original: "evaporir"</note> from it for three weeks. Afterward, take it out and let it become dry in the air or in the sun; thus you will finally obtain an **Azure** <note>original: "Azurium"; a blue pigment</note>, of which one **lot** <note>a weight of approximately 15 grams</note> is worth four **florins** or **guilders** in money.

## Angel’s Hand or Angel’s Blood Salt, which performs better than all else
Seek a **root** <note>original: "Radic. erbitt"</note> when the Sun is in the heavenly sign of **Leo**. Then take the juice of the **herb of bark**, mix the same together, and distill it here three times through an **alembic** <note>a distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>. Then take one part of **Endowed Earth** <note>original: "Terræ indatæ"</note> and grind it very small; also take seven parts of **fennel leaves** <note>original: "fynschelen laub"</note> very finely, and thus prepare the **Blood** <note>original: "Sanguinem oder Blut"</note>. And set it under **manure** <note>original: "Mist"; used as a steady, natural heat source for fermentation</note> for 14 or 26 days. Afterward, distill it again through an **alembic**, and keep it properly until you have reached its **grade** <note>proper strength or concentration</note> for your **operations** or works.

## An Oil for the Liver of St. Thomas
Take old and the best **olive oil**, as much as you wish. Add to it a third part of **fixed Sal Ammoniac** <note>sal ammoniac that has been treated to withstand heat without sublimating</note>, and a third part of **salt of tartar** <note>potassium carbonate</note> likewise. Grind them all together at once upon a **marble stone**, and set them under warm **horse manure** for 17 days. Afterward, distill them in the glass, in such a way that you first give them a **gentle fire**, and afterward increase the fire.

can one also handle all other **spirits**, such
as **frankincense** <note>original: "Weihrauch"</note>, so it will become
firm thereby, and endure in the fire or
the **tests** <note>original: "Proben"</note>.

# A Sublimation of Sulfur

Take well-purified **Sulfur**, and grind
it with strong **vinegar** for an entire day,
and take away the **impurity** <note>original: "Unflat"</note> which floats

<column-break/>

or swims just above it.
On the second day, however, **decoct** <note>boil down</note> it in **wine**,
and take away the impurity or thick vapor
that swims over it; when you have done this,
let it dry, and grind it, and
add to it an equal amount of prepared **saltpeter** <note>original: "Salnis"</note>,
and place them in a vessel for **sublimating** just
like the mercury. But you must not maintain such
a great fire as you did for the **sublimation**
of the **Mercury**, but rather the
**Sulfur** must be sublimated by a gentle fire
for an entire day.
Then you will find **sublimated** and **black Sulfur**. **Sublimate** it once
more with those same **dregs**, so
the **Sulfur** will become white. **Sublimate**
it for a third time with **salt**,
so it will become wonderfully fine white, so
that it may richly surpass the saltpeter
in regards to its **whiteness** <note>original: "Albedinem"</note>. Repeat,
however, its **sublimation** by
itself, while it is good, and keep it tightly sealed.

# Oil of Sulfur or "swimming oil" is made thus

Take **Sulfur** with common prepared
**salt**, and let it boil with **vinegar**,
thereafter distill it there in a
**glass retort** <note>original: "Verrestratt"</note> and a sealed vessel
until the material becomes entirely dry.
Thereafter grind it, and place it in a
**cucurbit** <note>original: "Cucurbitas"; the lower part of a distilling apparatus</note> or flask for distillation.
Distill it until nothing more comes out of it.

# Oil of Sulfur
Pulverize **sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> in a **crucible** <note>original: "Tigell"</note>, and add to it as much clear **glass** <note>Note: pulverized glass was often used as a flux or to provide surface area in alchemical reactions</note> as you wish. Thereafter, put all this material into a glass vessel and set it beneath the earth. Build a fire over it for three whole days and nights. This **oil** tinctures [metals] but krieg <note>likely "kriegt" or "reaches"</note> only into **gold** <note>original: "Solem"; the alchemical symbol for the sun representing gold</note>.

# A Congelation of Mercury
Take **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note>, red **living sulfur** <note>original: "Lebendigen schwebell rothm"</note> or **unused arsenic** <note>original: "Ungebrauchten Arsenicium"</note>, and **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "Sal Armoniack"</note>. Grind all these together with one another, and let them stand for a day and night in a damp place, ensuring that you grind them every day. After this, distill the water over an **alembic** <note>original: "Alembicum"; the hooded cap of a distilling apparatus</note> by or with a gentle fire; the water shall **congeal** <note>original: "congeliren"; to turn from a liquid to a solid or semi-solid state</note>.

# A Fairly Poor Mercury
### Not an All Too Good Mercury
Take **ceruse** <note>original: "Cerussam"; white lead pigment</note>, which has been extracted and drawn from lead sheets, and grind it upon a **marble stone**. **Distemper** <note>original: "distemperier"; to mix or thin a pigment with a binder</note> or mix it with water; thereafter, add to it the **sulfur water** mentioned above and let it become dry in the sun. It will become a very handsome white **ceruse** and a good, beautiful color. When you place this **ceruse** into a **cupel** <note>original: "Testam oder dachelschall"; a shallow clay vessel used for heating metals</note> and burn it with fire, you will find the very best **silver** <note>original: "Lunam"; the alchemical symbol for the moon representing silver</note>.

<column-break/>

# Oil of Tartar or Tartar
### Oil is Made Thus
Take crude **tartar** <note>original: "weinstein"; the hard potassium bitartrate crust that forms in wine barrels</note> and place it in a pot. Cover the same and seal it around the joint with **lute of wisdom** <note>original: "Luto sapientiae"; a hermetic sealing clay often made of earth, horse hair, and binders to prevent vapors from escaping</note>, and let it dry out. Thereafter, place such a pot in a **glass furnace** <note>original: "glashoffen"</note> for ten days. Finally, take it out and grind it, and lay it (the **tartar**) upon a **marble stone** in a damp place; thus you will have the **oil** <note>Note: This refers to "oil of tartar per deliquium," where the salt absorbs moisture from the air to form a concentrated liquid</note>. Place a glass under the **marble stone** into which the **oil** may flow or drip and be distilled from the marble stone. Should it not do so by itself, you must be skillful in your actions for your own profit.

# Wine of Sulfur or to Make
### Living Sulfur
Take hard **egg yolks** that have been boiled hard, and into which **wine** and **sulfur** <note>original: "schwebell"</note> have been placed. Mix these with one another, and thus you will obtain **living sulfur**.

### Alkali Salt is made thus
Take unslaked and unwashed lime, and lay it in a thick cloth, and pour boiling water into it, and let it coagulate like lye. Pour boiling water into it again afterward, until all bitterness <note>original: "Amaritudo"</note> is drawn out from the earth and the lime. Cast away the dregs <note>original: "faces"</note>, and prepare everything until you have enough water and a good portion. Then make it somewhat fatty <note>likely meaning to evaporate it to a thick or oily consistency</note> by heating the water in a crucible until it entirely disappears and yields neither vapor nor smoke. And from this, the stone is made which is called Alkali Stone <note>original: "Lapis Alkali"</note>. Then take salt and put it in a new vessel, and place it sealed in a furnace without a lid, and give it first a gentle fire

gentle fire, thereafter a heavy one, until it melts like wax. Then pour it quickly into a new basin, and you will find the alkali is well prepared. Note also that Alkali Salt <note>original: "Sal Alkali"</note> reduces all metallic bodies into an equal substance, and its nature is warm and dry.

### Now I must also speak of the preparation
of Arsenic, Orpiment, and Sulfur <note>original: "Arsenici, Auripigmenti und Sulphuris"</note>. Since these all are of and have a light nature, and serve this art greatly. Take sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> as much as you wish, and in contrast [soak] it with good, sharp wine vinegar for three or four days. When it is well-cooked <note>original: "coquiryt"</note> and poured, then take away the flask <note>original: "Urinal"; here referring to a rounded glass vessel</note> or thick vapor with a thread, which has floated down or through the drying process. Afterward let it become dry, and grind it on a stone with a little labor, and also with sharp vinegar <note>original: "Acet"</note> and wine. Lay it all in a vessel that is well-fired for that purpose, and set the vessel upon a furnace <note>original: "Fuernaß"</note>. Cover it with a vessel which is called a flask <note>original: "Urinal"</note>, and seal it well with clay or stone so that it does not breathe <note>leak</note> or run out. And the vessel shall have a hole at the top. When it has had enough, and when it is sufficiently sublimated <note>original: "sublimiret"</note>, you will find that the sulfur has colored and dyed itself very deeply.

### A Gradation of Gold so that
### it retains the ninth degree
<note>A "gradation" is an alchemical process intended to improve the color, purity, or "grade" of gold</note>

### How one should transform Silver into Gold

Take 1 ounce of fine burnt copper-lime <note>original: "Kupfer Kal"; likely copper oxide or calcined copper</note>, Sal Ammoniac <note>original: "Sal Armeniacum"; a common alchemical salt used as a flux</note>, in which there is one [part] Vitriol, and Crocus Martis <term>Crocus Martis</term> <note>A red iron oxide powder used for coloring and in transmutative recipes</note> in equal parts; pulverize them and mix them together with linseed oil. It will become a thick pitch-fat or melted silver. Let the third part of this be Gold; let them flow or melt together in a goldsmith’s crucible for one hour, etc.

### A water which reduces all metals into their first matter

Take the very best primary vinegar <term>Acetio</term>, Alum, cast glass <note>original: "geost glass"; possibly calcined glass or a specific glass flux</note>, Venice soap, and Sal Ammoniac in equal parts. Pulverize them all well, and dissolve <note>original: "drosquire"; likely from the Latin "distringere" or a variant of "dissolve"</note> them in vinegar with the metal. Thereafter, grind the metal and let it boil once in the mentioned vinegar, and then grind it again, up to three times or as long as it takes until the metal is ennobled <note>original: "Inaldirt"; likely referring to a surface change or "ennobling" the metal</note> or becomes white.

### An Augmentation <term>Augmentatio</term> for the increase of Sol.

<note>original: "Solis"; Latin for "of the Sun," the standard alchemical symbol for Gold.</note>

Take 1 ounce of Bismuth, 1 ounce of Cinnabar <note>original: "Zinnober"; mercury sulfide, prized for its deep red color</note>, and 1 ounce of sublimated Mercury. Sublimate these together as if everything remains at the bottom. Then take 1 ounce of Alum, 1 ounce of Vitriol, 1 ounce of Saltpeter <note>original: "Salis Nitrij"</note>, and 1 ounce of Sal Ammoniac. Grind all these together with the material as it was fixed above. Then take as many gold pieces as you wish, and first place a layer of filed gold on the bottom of the crucible.

## Tutty
<note>Tutty, or *Tutia*, was a term used for zinc oxide, often collected as a crust from the chimneys of smelting furnaces, used both medicinally and in metallurgy.</note>

Take shells or mussels, and crush and grind them as finely as possible. Do this three times: calcining and imbibing. ## A Calcination of Venus
<note>Venus is the alchemical name for copper.</note>

Take plates of Venus [copper] as large as a denarius or a small token coin, and moisten them with linseed oil and strew sublimated orpiment <term>Auripigmentum</term> <note>Arsenic trisulfide, a bright yellow mineral often used by alchemists in attempts to simulate the color of gold.</note> upon them. Put this into a vessel and arrange it layer by layer <note>original Latin: *S. S. S.* for *stratum super stratum*</note>. Set the vessel upon or in the burning or glowing coals in a calcining furnace, yet in such a way that it does not flow or melt. Let it stand in such heat or warmth for an entire day. Afterwards, take it out again, grind it well, and imbibe it with sharp vinegar. Then let it be for sublimation, until it is all completely sublimated. Then wash it well with hot water until the water comes away clean. Then grind it with oil of alkali salt <term>Oleo salis Alkali</term> <note>A caustic solution, likely potassium carbonate.</note>, and place it in a linen cloth. Polish or coat half the cloth—an ell's length—like a bale or a round ball with clay, which shall be mixed with horse manure, common salt, and egg whites. With such clay or loam, prepare the linen cloth fully, and let it go into a hole in the smelting hut.

### For Malleability

Take common purified salt that is well-cleaned, and a little of the red Crocus Martis <term>Crocus Martis</term> <note>A red iron oxide powder used for polishing and coloring.</note>, and also as much Saltpeter <note>original: "Sale Nitri"</note>—well-purified like the common salt—along with the Crocus Martis. ### A Sublimation of Arsenic

Take Arsenic, namely raw <note>original: "lebendigen"</note> arsenic, and soak it in good lead-vinegar <note>Vinegar in which lead has been dissolved, used for its chemical reactivity.</note>. Then imbibe <note>to soak or saturate</note> it three times with very sharp vinegar and mix it. Add one part of Sal Ammoniac or rust, and let it sublimate in a vessel suitable for this purpose. Pay diligent attention that you have a vessel that is sharp and pointed at the top. Move it into a small furnace that is also suited for it. Make a good, gentle fire for half a day; after that, make the fire underneath a little stronger, but not much stronger, for the work would be destroyed. Sublimate it thus over a gentle fire for an entire natural day—that is, day and night. Afterward, take it out and grind it again, and so on.

# In Calcination, it is to be noted
### and observed,
That the vessel belonging to the **Calcination** <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance—often a metal—to high temperatures in order to oxidize it or turn it into a fine powder.</note>
should be well sealed and the mouth closed,
so that it does not leak out, for the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"; the volatile, gaseous essence of the substance.</note>
is the most fleeting part of it, and then the
**Body** <note>original: "Corpus"; the physical, solid matter being worked upon.</note> cannot be brought to perfection. And
this is my **Secret** <note>original: "Secretum"; a personal or guarded alchemical discovery.</note>.

# Knowledge or
### Science
A hidden, naked, and dark **Science** <note>original: "Scientia"; here referring to the esoteric wisdom of alchemy rather than modern laboratory science.</note> or knowledge, in which divine
mysteries and secrets are found, through
which all things were first established,
which has the **face of a lion** <note>A common alchemical symbol representing the "Fixed" or the "Sulphur of the Wise," often associated with strength and the color red.</note>, and has a red
color, and within it is Earth, Fire,
Water, and Air.

### Knowledge
> Hidden, naked, and dark [knowledge] in which are divine

# A Congealing of Mercury
Take **Mercury**, living sulfur or
**rahnball**, red **Arsenic**, **Sal Armoniacum** <term>Sal Armoniacum</term> <note>Ammonium chloride; a salt used to clean metals and facilitate chemical reactions.</note>
in equal parts <note>original: "Ana"; an abbreviation indicating equal amounts of each ingredient.</note>. Grind these same materials well
together for 10 days, and let them sit for eight days
or so in a damp place, so
that this sulfur binds together. After this,
distill the water in an
**Alembic** <term>Alembic</term> <note>A classic distillation apparatus consisting of a gourd-like flask and a cooling cap with a delivery tube.</note> with a gentle or moderate
fire; the **mother** <note>likely the "mother liquor" or the residual liquid left after crystallization or distillation.</note> congeals the **Mercury**.

# How to make Mercury hard
### and malleable
Take the **Mercury**, and place it in a
metallic vessel and pour into it **Olive
Oil** or **Laurel Oil**, and let it boil
over a gentle fire, and be very careful
that the Mercury does not overflow
when you frequently pour oil in, namely
five or six times. When the oil
has dried up, finally pour in
**distilled Vinegar** <note>original: "sublimirten Acetum"; vinegar that has been purified through distillation.</note> and let
the Mercury boil in it until it is
completely dried up. Thus the **Mercury**
will then become hard and malleable.

## Follows the Solution of this Stone

Place the vial in **dung** <note>original: "Mist"; a common alchemical method for providing steady, gentle warmth through the natural heat of fermentation</note> for 6 weeks, in such a way that the neck is half-way out of the dung; thus it will be dissolved into a red water. Afterward, **coagulate** <note>solidify</note> this same water through the heat or warmth of the sun. And this is indeed a magnificent composition of the stone, of which I can truly say that in the whole world no other has been found to equal it, and many **philosophers** <note>alchemists</note> have sought such a stone /

---

## Follows Concerning its Projection
<note>"Projection" is the final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" or Elixir is thrown upon a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</note>

Take an assaying crucible <note>original: "probierkorn dem Tiegel"</note> and put within it 70 parts of **raw mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij crudi"</note>. Then place the crucible upon or in the glowing coals and let the mercury become very warm. Afterward, take 1 part of the aforementioned stone and throw it onto the warmed mercury; the stone or **elixir** will run through all the members of the mercury and penetrate it, and it will give birth to or dye it into the color of silver and **perfect Luna** <note>original: "Vollkommmenen Lünam"; pure silver</note>. Do not fail to help and remember the poor and needy for God's sake.

### Recipe for good ink or black ink

Take two ounces <note>℥</note> of **oak galls** <note>original: "Gallen de stall von Ven:"; likely high-quality Aleppo galls imported via Venice, used for their tannin content</note>, one ounce of **Roman vitriol** <note>iron sulfate, the second key ingredient in iron gall ink</note>, half an ounce of **gum arabic**, and as much water as you see is necessary.

### Several problems concerning the gall follow

First is the question of why animals have a **gall** <note>referring to both the gallbladder and the bile within it</note>. Here is the answer: the gall is a well-mixed **humor** <term>humor: one of the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to govern health</term> which, with its sharpness and biting bitterness, greatly benefits the intestines and bowels, for it drives out the superfluous and useless matter and helps the stomach to **digest** <note>original: "dauen"</note> the food, etc.

Furthermore, there is the question of why animals suffer from **colic** <note>original: "pasio"; likely *passio iliaca*, a severe intestinal blockage</note> or **intestinal gout** <note>original: "darm gicht"</note>, as well as **diarrhea** <note>original: "Diarrhea"</note>, which arises and comes from the settling of the gall. To this it is answered: the nature and movement of the gall humor is normally moderated and settled, though it is bitter. Now, if the openings of the **small gallbladder** <note>original: "Bladlins der Gallen"</note> are blocked, then that same humor cannot reach its proper place or enter the bladder. It must then instead flow out into the nourishment and food of the entire human **body** <note>original: "Coerpers"</note>. Just as [nourishment] is distributed here and there throughout the whole body, the bile is also distributed; yet, because of the bitterness of the mixed-in gall, it is not accepted as nourishment. Instead, it gnaws through the entire body and infects or poisons the skin.
